articles.title: Tom Skerritt, Alien and Top Gun actor, dies at 93
articles.summary:
The actor, who also had roles in M*A*S*H, A River Runs Through It and Picket Fences, dies of natural causes

Tom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien and Top Gun, has died at the age…

blocks.text: Tom Skerritt, the actor known for roles in Alien and Top Gun, has died at the age of 93.
His publicist confirmed to Variety that he died from natural causes.

“While the world knew Tom through his remarkable acting career, we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity, and the love he brought into our lives,” a family statement shared with People read.
In a career spanning more than 60 years, the actor had more than 170 big and small screen credits, winning an Emmy and receiving Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild award nominations.

After serving a four-year tour of duty in the US air force, Skerritt made his big-screen debut in the 1962 war film War Hunt alongside Robert Redford and Sydney Pollack, but his breakout came in 1970 with a role in Robert Altman’s hit satire M*A*S*H. The film was a major box office hit and was nominated for the best picture Oscar.

The 1970s saw Skerritt follow the film with roles in the cult black comedy Harold and Maude, Altman’s crime drama Thieves Like Us, Roger Corman’s sexploitation comedy Big Bad Mama and the Oscar-nominated ballet drama The Turning Point.

blocks.caption: Sigourney Weaver, Yaphet Kotto, John Hurt, Tom Skerritt and Ian Holm in Alien. Photograph: Ronald Grant

blocks.text: The decade closed out with a role in Ridley Scott’s smash hit Alien, a film he had earlier turned down due to the low budget. “At two million bucks and with other actors that I don’t know about, this is a film that could have been directed by Ed Wood,” he said in a 2019 interview. “I was uncertain about it because my training with Altman and Ashby had proceeded me, so I had that approach that I had absorbed from watching those two guys going about their work.”
The following decade saw him feature in David Cronenberg’s The Dead Zone, the sci-fi adventure SpaceCamp, horror sequel Poltergeist III and female-led comedy drama Steel Magnolias.

Skerritt also worked with Tony Scott in the 1986 blockbuster Top Gun, a role he almost didn’t get. “There was some question about me playing that role because I was … I think they used the word, laconic,” he said in a 2021 interview with Vulture. “It pissed me off. I went into it with [producer] Don Simpson, who was still alive at that point … don’t tell me, as a producer, what you think I’m going to be doing. You’re going to get what you need.”
In the 1990s, he reunited with Robert Redford for A River Runs Through It and also starred with Jodie Foster in Contact, Drew Barrymore in Poison Ivy and Diane Keaton in The Other Sister.
Skerritt also received an Emmy for his role in David E Kelley’s family drama Picket Fences, a show that ran for four seasons.
The 2000s saw him star with Bruce Willis in Tears of the Sun, Kate Beckinsale in Whiteout and on the small screen he had roles in Will & Grace, The West Wing and Brothers & Sisters.
His last film role was in the western drama Broke in 2025 with Dennis Quaid.

In 2012, he also co-founded an initiative called the Red Badge Project, which aimed to help veterans process their PTSD through storytelling. “It starts with that wanting to help someone else rather than talking about it,” Skerritt said to CBS News. “I just got tired of talking about this if I could do something about it.”
“I’m just a lucky guy, man,” he said in 2021. “Strength is measured in how you confront your weaknesses. I have had a lot of weaknesses. I still have them.”

articles.title: Teacher wounded in Oregon school shooting played dead after she was shot
articles.summary:
Becky Drury says she was hit by gunfire before she could intervene in attack that killed four, including three children

A teacher wounded in

blocks.text: A teacher wounded in last week’s shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school shared her account of the incident, and how she was shot before she could intervene and “[pretended] to be dead”.

Becky Drury was seriously wounded at Silver Rail elementary when Griffin J John II, a 16-year-old former student at the school armed with a shotgun, broke in and headed toward a special education classroom. He shot six people, killing Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher, and three children, including five-year-old Rhoam Summer.
Drury and Saylor Graham, a seven-year-old student, were also shot. Another teacher threw her phone at John and tackled him before a parent fatally shot the teen gunman.
Drury, who is still hospitalized, released a statement on Wednesday.

“Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on. I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there. Before I could do anything more, he shot me at close range and I fell to the ground,” Drury said.
Her left hand was almost completely severed, and her other arm was also badly injured, Drury said.

“I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else. So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again,” she said. “I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act.”

Drury’s account contradicted some reporting that she had thrown herself on top of a student in an effort to protect her, and the 54-year-old said she wanted to ensure “the events of that day and my actions in particular are reported accurately”.
She described the violence as “unimaginable” and said “my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy.”
Public schools in the central Oregon city began reopening this week. Dozens of officers have welcomed students as they return to their classes.
The shooting remains under investigation. The Bend police department said this week that the shotgun used in the incident was purchased legally.

articles.title: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing
articles.summary:
Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years

The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were…

blocks.text: The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing.

The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks.

The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs.

This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures that came into force in the mid-2010s, in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash.

The senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, it was later expanded to cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds.

It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helped lift the cap on banker bonuses, which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary.

The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls.

Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers.
after newsletter promotion

The regulators said removing these “unnecessary burdens” would save businesses about £2bn over 10 years while cutting the Bank of England’s and FCA’s costs by £11.5m and £229m each year, respectively.

The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. They said in a joint statement that the “high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers”.

articles.title: Aipac halts candidate endorsements amid US backlash against Israel
articles.summary:
‘Political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability’

When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in…

blocks.text: When the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most prominent pro-Israel lobby group in the US, announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates or make direct contributions to them, its many critics were quick to hail the development as Aipac’s admission of how toxic its brand had become.

The announcement marked a significant reversal that underscored just how profoundly US public opinion of Israel has shifted over the latest war in Gaza, and how political candidates’ once reflexive support for Israel has increasingly become a liability.

But Aipac, which only launched its political action committee and started endorsing candidates three cycles ago, is hardly getting out of US elections. It pledged to maintain the work of its deep-pocketed super pac, United Democracy Project, and to continue to funnel millions of dollars to prop up pro-Israel candidates through individual donors and Aipac members. The shift in strategy was a sign it was adapting to a changing political landscape, not that it was giving up its efforts to shape it.

“Historically, AIPAC sustained an aura of invincibility that ensured it won most battles by walkover – if you are perceived as invincible, the other side doesn’t even bother to fight you,” the political analyst Trita Parsi wrote. “Rather than invincibility, AIPAC’s name now carries such toxicity that the group doesn’t want its own name on its political donations.”

Aipac did not respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Aipac, which normally backs Democrats, was planning to give as much as $9m to a Pac supporting Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. The group had already spent $32m seeking to defeat El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, in the primaries.

But the announcement that it would stop directly backing candidates going forward was seen as tacit recognition that Aipac’s open support risked hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them.

“Through this shift, AIPAC openly admitted that their brand has become toxic in the political world,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, one of Aipac’s most vocal critics, told the Guardian. “Fewer and fewer candidates are willing to be publicly affiliated with this extremist, warmongering group. This is a clear signal: being pro-genocide is bad politics and bad policy.”

In a letter from Aipac to members first reported on by Jewish Insider, the group’s leadership seemed to acknowledge that its once formidable power in US elections had suffered as more candidates openly distanced themselves from Israel, and from the group itself. In the letter, they noted that the 2026 election was “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory” for the group and predicted that the “challenges we are confronting will continue to grow in the years ahead.”

“To win the fight for the future of the country and the U.S.-Israel alliance, we must build a more strategic, consequential, and nimble political operation,” they wrote. “The only tactic we’re married to is the most effective one.”

While Aipac boasted that it helped 290 candidates this election cycle, leading to the defeat of 29 candidates it described as “anti-Israel”, the group has also suffered major blows – including in Michigan and New Jersey. More than a dozen candidates who took Aipac contributions in the past have since publicly distanced themselves from the group, and New York’s rep Pat Ryan announced last week that he would return nearly $250,000 from the group, the latest of several elected officials to return Aipac funds or say they would turn it down.

Dion Nissenbaum, a journalist whose documentary on Aipac was published this week, featuring interviews with former Aipac insiders, told the Guardian that the announcement appeared to be the “first real admission from Aipac that their campaign strategy has backfired”.
Still, he warned, “if Aipac’s super PAC – the main source of its campaign donations – is going to keep operating, it may be an attempt to reinvent itself without ceding the battlefield.”

Tuesday’s announcement would change little in practice, those who have monitored Aipac’s political funding say. An Aipac spokesperson told Jewish Insider that Aipac members had contributed over $90m to candidates this election cycle – far more than the $3m in donations the group contributed directly through its Pac.
“This is not new,” Hady Amr, a former secretary for Israeli and Palestinian affairs with the US state department, noted. “This is Aipac going back to their tried and true approach.”

Groups like TrackAipac and initiatives like the Reject Aipac campaign, that have in recent years played a growing role in calling out candidates over their ties to the group, are already attuned to the varied avenues through which the pro-Israel lobby funnelled contribution to candidates, some more visible than others.

“[Aipac] has already been experimenting with ways to make their support more untraceable,” said Hamid Bendaas of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, one of the groups behind the Reject Aipac campaign. By dropping endorsements and direct contributions, Aipac was giving up one tool available to lobby organizations to signal to politically-aligned donors who may not be active members which candidates to back. Aipac had calculated that approach was more risky than worth it, he added, but it had plenty of other tools available.

“It’s akin to an animal that chews its leg off to get out of a bear trap. It’s a last resort choice to survive and stay relevant, which they will on both counts,” Bendaas added. “Aipac is going to continue influencing elections. If you’re someone who wants Aipac out of politics entirely, this is not that.

“We know they’re going to continue driving tens of millions of dollars into our elections to support Israel’s atrocities,” echoed Miller, of JVP. “And we will continue to fight to fully get them, and their dirty money, out of our politics and out of Congress.”

articles.title: Canada Post starting weekend parcel delivery in Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa this fall
articles.summary: Canada's national mail carrier says it plans to start delivering parcels on the weekend to seven million households by the end of 2027, as part of the financially troubled Crown corporation's major…

image.caption: A Canada Post employee returns to a delivery depot in Vancouver following a month-long national strike in December 2024. The corporation says it's starting to see signs of recovery as customers return following years of uncertainty. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada's national mail carrier says it plans to start delivering parcels on the weekend to seven million households by the end of 2027, as part of the financially troubled Crown corporation's major restructuring.
Financially troubled Crown corporation gives update on restructuring
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 22, 2026 3:44 PM EDT | Last Updated: 13 minutes ago
Canada's national mail carrier says it has begun delivering parcels on the weekend to homes in Ottawa and Montreal, with plans to expand to Toronto in late November.
The financially troubled Crown Corporation also says it plans to provide weekend delivery to other urban centres like Vancouver, Edmonton and Calgary next year.
It aims to offer weekend delivery to seven million households by the end of 2027.

Private carriers have successfully outpaced Canada Post by offering weekend and evening delivery for years. Until recently, the Crown corporation had said it was unable to do the same because of the previous collective agreement it had with its mail carriers.
Senior leadership provided an update on Canada Post's restructuring efforts and finances during its annual public meeting on Thursday.
Canada Post continues to lose money, including $482 million in the first half of 2026 before tax. Leadership said they expect the company will still need to rely on federal loans to stay afloat.

Canada Post employees and supporters rally at Canada Post headquarters in Ottawa during the November 2024 national strike that completely shut down mail service in the country. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

"The continued reliance on government funding is not a long-term solution and we are committed to reduce the reliance on government support as quickly as we can," said Rindala El-Hage, Canada Post's chief financial officer.
Despite the continued losses, Canada Post is showing signs of early recovery, El-Hage said, as customers return after a long period of labour disruption.
Parcel revenue grew by 20.7 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. Operating costs also declined by $119 million.
The Canadian Union of Postal Workers (CUPW) and the corporation signed a new collective agreement in June which stays in effect until 2030.

articles.title: Trump attacks Ohio governor over call for Ramaswamy to drop ‘deeply troubling’ ad
articles.summary:
Republican Mike DeWine says Ramaswamy ‘wrong’ to run controversial ad, drawing swift rebuke from president

Ohio’s Republican governor Mike DeWine on Thursday said gubernatorial candidate…

blocks.text: Ohio’s Republican governor Mike DeWine on Thursday said gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy was “wrong” to release an ad critical of his Democratic rival Amy Acton that featured her estranged mother, and implored Ramaswamy to take the ad down.
DeWine’s comments drew a swift rebuke from Donald Trump, who urged Ramaswamy to keep the ad up.

Acton, who has led the Republican nominee Ramaswamy in recent polls of the governor’s race, has said she has not seen her mother Donna Arthur for decades, after she married a man who sexually abused her when she was 12 years old and stayed with him even after police stepped in.
Calling the ad “deeply, deeply troubling”, DeWine told reporters at the Ohio state capital. “It’s wrong to run this ad,” the Associated Press reported.
“I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down,” the governor added.

The video, which began circulating on social media earlier this week and Ramaswamy’s campaign later told Ohio media outlets is their work, shows Arthur calling her daughter “a liar” and saying she should not be put in charge of the state. Ramaswamy’s campaign said later in the week it would spend $4m to air the ad across the state.

DeWine noted that “family members have always historically been off limits” and Acton had earlier this year mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother’s involvement in an alleged “pump and dump” scheme, though with less prominence than the Ramaswamy ad.
On Truth Social Thursday afternoon, Trump excoriated DeWine for his comments, saying DeWine was “disloyal to the Republican party”.

“He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn’t want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing,” Trump wrote. “I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!”

Connie Luck, a spokesperson for the Republican’s campaign, said: “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards when Democrats have regularly used family members of President Trump, RFK Jr, and other Republicans in ads. Voters shouldn’t buy it.”
Speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Wednesday, vice-president JD Vance dismissed criticism of Ramaswamy’s campaign. “Whether the ad was appropriate or not is not really my concern,” Vance said.

“I’m a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America. Politics is a tough business.”

In a statement released by Acton’s campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, called the ad “a despicable low” for Ramaswamy, and noted that he and his sister were removed from Arthur’s custody after her stepfather was arrested.

Republican US senator Jon Husted, who is facing a election bid that could decide which party controls the chamber in the 3 November midterm elections, joined in the condemnation. “I would not have run that ad,” he told the Associated Press.
His Democratic opponent, former senator Sherrod Brown, has called the video “disgusting”, and said all candidates should denounce it.

Ohio’s Republican secretary of state Frank LaRose also criticized Ramaswamy, telling Columbus-area broadcaster ABC 6: “I probably wouldn’t run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision.”
DeWine nonetheless declined to drop his endorsement of Ramaswamy in the governor’s race, saying he wanted to support the “full ticket” of Republican candidates in the midterms.

articles.title: Canadian diplomats based in U.S. advised to avoid appearing with midterm candidates
articles.summary: The government of Canada has issued advice to all embassy and consulate staff to avoid appearing with U.S. midterm candidates, according to a source with knowledge of the notices.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford participate in a joint news conference on Wednesday. Both were asked about recent accusations from U.S. officials that Canada is potentially meddling in the midterm elections. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The government of Canada has issued advice to all embassy and consulate staff to avoid appearing with U.S. midterm candidates, according to a source with knowledge of the notices.
Global Affairs Canada says issuing advice to diplomats around elections is routine
Two separate notices were sent out in the last month, the source said.
Those instructions, which Global Affairs Canada describes as routine, come as Trump administration officials level accusations of "potential interference in U.S. elections" at Canadian officials.

In addition, the source said the government told diplomatic staff to be careful with their social media, not pick sides and not pose for photos with candidates. Bloomberg first reported news of the government notices.
The source characterized the advice as basic reminders.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown

blocks.text: "As part of regular business, Global Affairs Canada provides instructions to its Canadian missions abroad. Government officials are always instructed to limit public events and stakeholder engagement during election periods in their host country," a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada separately told CBC News.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" on Wednesday that lists a number of instances it alleges could amount to "potential" interference, including a reference to Bernadette Jordan, Canada's consul general in Boston, appearing at a Canada-U.S. trade event with Democratic candidates last week.
Carney, Ford respond to Trump administration's election interference claims
The source told CBC News that the most recent bulletin was sent out last week before the U.S. Embassy issued its statement.

The embassy statement came after two Trump administration officials — trade adviser Peter Navarro and U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra — warned Canadians not to get involved in the U.S. midterms.

Hoekstra specifically mentioned Industry Minister Mélanie Joly in his comments on potential meddling. Four of the nine instances listed in the embassy release also reference Joly's comments about Canada's counter-tariff strategy, going back to March 2025 when she was in charge of foreign affairs.
Joly has pushed back on assertions that she's trying to influence the midterms and did so again on Thursday, saying she has met with both Republicans and Democrats during recent trips to the U.S.
"That is diplomacy, that's what we do," she told reporters during a news conference in Toronto.
Minister denies U.S. election interference claims by Trump administration
The embassy's recent release also mentions the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Regan ad that ran in the U.S. last year and comments made by Premier Doug Ford.
Both Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford were asked about the embassy's statement during a news conference on Wednesday. Both denied that they're trying to sway the vote south of the border.
"The United States initiated a series of trade actions. We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.
"All of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy."
Ford followed up by saying he has "no interest at all interfering in American elections."
"We're going to focus on what we can do here in Ontario and in Canada to make sure we protect our economy, protect the people and protect communities," the premier said.
Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms
The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates in border states like Michigan and Maine.
The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a new 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.
"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.
Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997, has also tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Katie Simpson and Kate McKenna

articles.title: Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
articles.summary: As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

image.caption: The response to Albania's protests has turned increasingly violentImage: Olsi Shehu/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.
Why Albania's political crisis is deepening
Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."
She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

blocks.caption: Anti-corruption protester "Sara" says communication occurs onlineImage: Kristi Çavo/DW

blocks.text: Rama: 'Hybrid war'

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

blocks.caption: A protester hurls back a tear gas canister fired at students by policeImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."
Is Rama deflecting?

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."

blocks.caption: Arlind Qori says the protesters are voicing legitimate demandsImage: Kristi Çavo/DW

blocks.text: "People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.
"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
articles.summary: Lina Attalah, who is accused of managing a website without a license, will go to court next week. Mada Masr has published reporting critical of Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.

image.caption: Lina Attalah, born in 1983, has years of journalism experience in Egypt and was previously the managing editor of the Egypt Independent online newspaper before the closure of its print edition [File Photo: 2020]Image: Khaled Desouki/AFP

blocks.text: Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution sent Mada Masr journalist Lina Attalah to stand for trial, the independent Egyptian news website said Thursday.

One of Madr Masar's co-founders, Attalah serves as the site's editor-in-chief. The website, which publishes in both Arabic and English, frequently features critical reporting related to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.
What do we know so far?
Prosecutors questioned Attalah for six hours on Wednesday in New Cairo, Mada Masr said.

She is accused of running a website without a license and the publication of false news "with the aim of disturbing public peace." Under questioning, the latter allegation was dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.
The trial has been referred to a New Cairo misdemeanors court and is slated to begin on October 27.
Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr's legal counsel, said there was "haste" in the trial referral and said the trial beginning next week signals "unjustified urgency."
Al-Azhari said Attalah could face a financial penalty of between 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (around €16,000 to €48,000; $18,000 to $54,000) if convicted.
Mada Masr said the organization has sought a license from the Egyptian government to run its news website since 2018 — the same year Egypt passed and ratified a law to regulate the press.

Egyptian authorities have been unresponsive over the past years to Mada Masr's attempts to procure a license, with Mada Masr later finding out in 2022 that its request was rejected. The site filed a lawsuit in 2022 and found out in 2023 that the rejection was due to missing documents.

The proceedings against Attalah come after Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists last month for independent fact-checking and investigative website Matsadaash (Egyptian Arabic for "don't believe").
Press freedom groups condemn actions against Attalah
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed alarm about Attalah's referral to trial.

"Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns in years, which began with the arrest of the six Matsdaash journalists," the CPJ's director for Middle East and North Africa Sara Qudah said. "It is long past time for Egypt to end this campaign and allow independent media to report freely."
Reporters without Borders (RSF) had earlier said it was alarmed by prosecutors' questioning of Attalah.

According to RSF's World Press Freedom Index, Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries, with many of the country's biggest news outlets either state-owned or controlled by wealthy businessmen who submit to the will of the government.

Egyptian President el-Sissi came to power in a 2013 military coup against Islamist President Mohamed Morsi. Since then, el-Sissi has cracked down and blocked websites such as Qatar's Al Jazeera and The New Arab on allegations of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.

articles.title: 96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
articles.summary: Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are at risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change the biggest threat. A new study found that 96% of reef systems are critically endangered.

image.caption: Australia's Great Barrier Reef is among those threatened Image: Norbert Probst/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.
In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.
Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.
Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.

"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.

blocks.caption: Coral reefs are home to a high level of biodiversityImage: Yuddy Cahya Budiman/REUTERS

blocks.text: What are the threats to the reefs?
Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).
Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.
This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.
Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.

When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.

blocks.caption: Sea turtles are among the animals that depend on coral reefsImage: Great Barrier Reef Foundation/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the reefs still be saved?

"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.

The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.

Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.
"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.

"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."

"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

articles.title: Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises
articles.summary:
Be Ready campaign aims to prepare UK for impact of climate crisis, technological dependency and threats by hostile state


Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of…

blocks.text: Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.

The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependancy and hostile state threats.

Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
“Terms like hybrid warfare and grey zone threats do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as state-sponsored terrorism,” he said.

“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.

“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”

People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.

The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.

Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to be prepared for serious disruption.

Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.

There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.

The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken off line in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.
after newsletter promotion

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependancy that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.

Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.

People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.

The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.

Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.

European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.

Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.

articles.title: Energy secretary appears to U-turn on opposition to tougher migration rules
articles.summary:
Miatta Fahnbulleh says reference to ‘awkward’ interview was meant to be lighthearted and self-deprecating

The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s…

blocks.text: The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.

Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”

The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.

Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.

“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.

Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.

blocks.caption: The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, arrives in Downing Street to attend the weekly Cabinet meeting on Tuesday. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Shutterstock

blocks.text: She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.

However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”

This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
after newsletter promotion

One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.

“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.

MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.

Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”

Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

articles.title: Detroit tourism bureau halts advertising in Canada amid trade war, hopes Canadians won't 'hold grudge'
articles.summary: Detroit’s tourism bureau has completely stopped marketing to Canada, saying they understand that the “antagonistic” American actions have strained relations between the two countries.

image.caption: Fewer people are visiting Detroit from Canada since a trade war between the two countries began, according to Tourism Detroit. (Jason Viau/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Detroit’s tourism bureau has completely stopped marketing to Canada, saying they understand that the “antagonistic” American actions have strained relations between the two countries.
'I can understand why Canadians are upset with us and I don’t hold that against Canadians'
Historically, Visit Detroit spent seven figures annually, which is about 10 per cent of its budget, trying to lure Canadians across the border.

Once tensions settle between the two nations, Visit Detroit said “we are so ready” to welcome Canadians back and don’t “begrudge” those who are avoiding U.S. travel, according to president & CEO Claude Molinari.

“I don’t think it’s unpatriotic to point out that a lot of the federal government policies of the United States that have been, to a certain degree, antagonistic toward Canada have impacted us negatively,” said Molinari.
Over the last two years, Visit Detroit said there’s been a 30 per cent drop in Canadians coming into their jurisdiction, although there’s been a seven per cent bump in the last two months.

“I can understand why Canadians are upset with us and I don’t hold that against Canadians,” said Molinari. “When the situation, I hope, normalizes in the very near future, that we’ll be able to welcome our Canadian friends back and they will not hold a grudge,” said Molinari.
Claude Molinari is the president and CEO of Visit Detroit. (Jason Viau/CBC)
In the meantime, Visit Detroit has re-routed the marketing dollars once spent in Canada in an attempt to bring people from Europe to the Motor City.
He said marketing efforts will resume in Canada when the issue of tariffs is resolved, and a greater level of “respect and positive relationship” exists between Ottawa and Washington.

U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed tariffs on a number of Canadian goods in recent months, which is particularly affecting Windsor's automotive industry in a big way. Canada has also introduced a number of retaliatory tariffs in response.
Ohio zoo holds annual Canadian appreciation day
Despite the tension, the Toledo Zoo in Ohio is forging ahead with a Canadian member appreciation day on Saturday.'

"We stay in our lane, which is animals and conservation and that's what our focus and our mission is and we welcome everyone to the zoo," said Tana Benford, vice president of development and membership at the Toledo Zoo.
It's an event for the more than 100 members offering them free perks, including a special lunch, to thank them for continuing to visit.
The Canadian event in Toledo first started after the COVID pandemic in response many of those members keeping memberships active despite not being able to cross the border.
"We're so glad and appreciative that [Canadians] have stuck with us ... some of the nicest, friendliest people" said
Even though the Canada-U.S. relationship is "strained," Molinari said he hope Canadians will return to Detroit land re-establish the historic connection.
"I don't want to be tone deaf and just assume 'ok all is forgiven, we're coming all back,'" said Molinari. “We miss our Canadian friends for sure."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Viau is reporter for CBC News based in Windsor, Ont. He has an interest in telling stories related to accountability, policing, court, crime and municipal affairs. You can email story ideas and tips to jason.viau@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Amy Winehouse musical in development for West End
articles.summary:
Stage show based on late singer reportedly set to feature her best-loved songs with involvement from her father Mitch

A musical based on

blocks.text: A musical based on Amy Winehouse is in development for London’s West End.

The project is still in early stages with Catherine Schreiber, a Tony award-winning producer (Cabaret, Rent), attached to the project, according to Variety. Casting is reported to currently be under way.
Mitch Winehouse, the late musician’s father, is also said to be involved with the show, indicating that it will probably feature her most loved songs.
The Guardian has approached Amy Winehouse’s record label for comment.

This week, the 20th anniversary of her landmark album Back to Black was celebrated with a tribute concert at London’s Roundhouse featuring performances by Jorja Smith, Mark Ronson, Lianne La Havas and Corinne Bailey Rae.
“Back to Black remains a miraculous set of modern love songs in vintage clothing,” wrote the Guardian’s Dorian Lynskey, adding that “re-enactments can be limiting”.
On 23 October, an expanded reissue of Back to Black will be released, including four unreleased demos, B-sides and a live album recording at Amsterdam’s Paradiso in 2007.
Mitch Winehouse has hinted at the possibility of a musical based on the singer over the years.

“A musical celebrating her life and music is being talked about for the near future,” he said in a 2017 interview. “It is something I’d really like to happen, and I’ve said I’m happy for it to go ahead.
“It would be for the West End. We want to do something that remembers Amy for what she was; there’s so much more to her than just the drugs and the alcohol.”
That is now set to come to fruition, joining the multiple posthumous music releases, films and TV specials that have been released since Winehouse’s death in 2011, aged 27.

In 2011, the rarities collection Lioness was received as a “flawed memorial for a flawed star”, while Sam Taylor-Johnson’s 2024 biopic of the musician was slammed as a “grotesque insult” by the Guardian’s Laura Snapes.

Meanwhile, Asif Kapadia’s 2015 documentary about the singer won the best documentary Oscar, and was praised by the Guardian as “an intimate and passionate tribute, tracing the awful trajectory of her celebrity destiny”.

A current London exhibition by the artist Alex Margo Arden assembles ephemera from Winehouse’s life in a Chelsea apartment, with items including ballet flats laid in tribute to the singer and a birthday card from Ronson and Adele that she never had the chance to open.

articles.title: Meta board placates Zuckerberg after threat to leave California if voters approve wealth tax measure
articles.summary: Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg, Reuters has reported, in a move spurred by a California ballot measure, part of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, that has sparked heated debate and…

image.caption: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg listens to U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on Sept. 29 in Washington, D.C. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg, Reuters has reported, in a move spurred by a California ballot measure, part of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, that has sparked heated debate and hundreds of millions in campaign spending.
Polls suggest a tight result on Prop 40, as some tech barons threaten to move out of state if it passes

Under the deal, Zuckerberg will get non-voting shares he can sell to potentially foot a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event the proposal is ​approved, in exchange for a commitment to remain a ​resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday.

Zuckerberg, the world's sixth richest person ​according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence ⁠outside California because Proposition ⁠40, the ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth ‌tax," could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it.

Proposition 40 asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5 per cent tax on the state's billionaires, and needs over 50 per cent support to pass. The state is home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively worth upwards of $2 trillion US.
State health care programs would be the biggest beneficiaries of proceeds raised through the fund, with money also going to state food assistance programs and public education.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign

blocks.text: The parent company of Facebook and Instagram said Zuckerberg needs to continue to manage the company from its Menlo Park headquarters at a time of "unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry." Meta says it needs to ⁠raise "hundreds ⁠of billions of dollars" over several ​years to ​finance its AI-related growth ⁠plan.

Meta will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027. Zuckerberg, who has a net worth of ‌about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20 per cent of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10 per cent of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill from Prop 40 without losing voting control.
Brin equates tax to Soviet-style oppression

Backers say California's measure would generate $100 billion US for health care, food assistance and education. But skeptics peg the revenue estimate at closer to $40 billion US and say it could also drive some billionaires ‌out of ⁠the state, depriving California of future tax revenue and investment.
Sergey Brin, Google co-founder, has spent more than $100 million US to defeat the ballot measure.

"I fled socialism with my family in 1979 and know the devastating, oppressive society it created in the Soviet Union. I don't want California to end up in the same place," Brin recently told the New York Times.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin is shown on Oct. 8 during an event at the U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C. Brin has spent millions trying to defeat California's Proposition 40 ballot measure. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Darien Shanske, a law professor at the University of California-Davis, who helped draft the proposal, told CNBC that relocating wouldn't limit the tax exposure of the ultra wealthy. Any billionaire residing in the state on Jan. 1, would still be taxed, given the state's tax laws, he said.
Prop 40 is supported by, among others, California Democrat Ro Khanna in the House of Representatives and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

"Are we destined to live in an oligarchic society begging for crumbs while our economic and political lives are controlled by a handful of the wealthiest people on Earth?" Sanders said at a rally in California earlier this month.
LISTEN | The latest on the midterms from our Washington correspondents:
Two Blocks from the White House34:00What Trump's very bad week might mean for the midterm races
Passage of the measure far from certain
The measure hasn't elicited a tidy split of progressives and Democrats in favour versus billionaires against, however.
Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, for example, has shrugged off the proposal.

"The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege," Huang told CBS News earlier this week. "I feel it's a privilege. It's a responsibility. And nothing would give me more joy than to be able to pay even more taxes."
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, seen at a Los Angeles campaign stop on Oct. 15, doesn't believe Proposition 40 is an adequate way to fund state services. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

Meanwhile, outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes Prop 40 and backs the Brin-introduced Proposition 42, which would seek to amend the state constitution to ban such tax proposals after Jan. 1, 2026.

Newsom's position earned a rebuke from outspoken actor Mark Ruffalo, who called it "beyond sad" on social media. Messaging directly to Newsom's account, Ruffalo said Democrats need someone who is "tough when it comes to the real imbalances people are struggling with every day: billionaires vs. people and the planet."

But current Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and the California Teachers Association (CTA) are also among the individuals and groups opposed to the measure, arguing that while well-intentioned, it is a complex and unsustainable funding measure. The CTA is focused on Proposition 3, which would raise funds through a state income tax hike on high earners.
Becerra's Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, is staunchly opposed to Prop 40.

items: Trump's complaints of 'rigged' L.A. mayoral vote could offer preview of midterm election night

blocks.text: California voters have only approved one in three citizen initiatives historically. As well, California ballot measures typically need robust early support, political analysts say, as history has shown the undecided are more apt to choose No when it comes to time to vote.

"California ballot measures tend to lose support over time, and if it's polling below 50 per cent in August, that's not a good sign for its prospects," John Pitney, a ​professor of politics at Claremont McKenna College, told Reuters in a report published Sept. 30.
A Citrin-Politico poll released this week indicated that, of those who took a position, 46 per cent of survey respondents favoured Prop 40 while 43 per cent were opposed.
