articles.title: NBI: P3.5 billion shabu from Laos points to Philippines network
articles.summary: The foiled smuggling of 521 kilograms of suspected shabu valued at P3.5 billion from Laos demonstrated how huge the Philippines’ drug market is and the sophisticated system that attempted…

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am

Ross Jonathan Galicia, who heads the NBI’s Dangerous Drugs Division, told House lawmakers their investigation indicated a local distribution network was behind it, with enormous resources, huge funds and networks that cross boundaries.
PNA / File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The foiled smuggling of 521 kilograms of suspected shabu valued at P3.5 billion from Laos demonstrated how huge the Philippines’ drug market is and the sophisticated system that attempted ttransport such volume by air, an official of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said yesterday.

“There is a local crime group that is operating within the country. It would take a number of people to move these illegal drugs. There’s a big market in the Philippines,” he said during a probe conducted by the House committee on dangerous drugs.
Galicia likewise said investigators must look beyond the drugs intercepted at Luang Prabang International Airport on Oct. 1 and examine the network that would have received and distributed them.
“Destination is the Philippines. We have established that,” he said, adding that those behind the operation had the funds to charter an aircraft and move the shipment quickly.

Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) director-general Isagani Nerez told the committee that they, along with the Philippine National Police, were building a case against individuals allegedly involved in financing, arranging and receiving the shipment.
The PDEA chief said investigators were gathering transaction documents covering the aircraft charter and seeking official investigation records from foreign counterparts.
The Bureau of Customs, however, said its own records had not yet established a Philippine recipient or importer.

Deputy Commissioner for intelligence Emmanuel Luis Licup reported that Customs found no notice of arrival for the aircraft and was still awaiting aviation, customs and investigation documents requested from Lao authorities.

“No verified Philippine consignee identified,” Licup said, presenting the bureau’s assessment. “The alleged Philippine destination remains under validation pending receipt of documentary evidence from foreign counterparts.”

The Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines also reported that an entry and exit permit had been requested for the aircraft, but the flight was never activated and the aircraft did not enter Philippine airspace.
Intensified search

Police have intensified their search for former Bangsamoro parliament member Edrieza Hadji Nasser Rimbang and four other people who snubbed subpoenas for them to shed light into the P3.5-billion shabu shipment from Laos.
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. has ordered police to find Rimbang, who was tagged as the financier of the foiled drug smuggling operation.
Rimbang, Abdulah Karim Macalatas, Abdullah Rimbang Macarimbang and Aldren Samante did not show up for the probe being conducted by the police Criminal Investigation and Detection Group.
For Nartatez, Rimbang and the other persons’ participation are necessary to establish the complete circumstances surrounding the drug shipment that was intercepted by Laotian authorities on Oct. 1.
The CIDG is wrapping up its probe and will submit a report of its investigation to Nartatez as early as today.
“The evidence gathered reflects a thorough, evidence-based approach aimed at establishing the truth and ensuring accountability,” he said.

The CIDG has issued over 40 subpoenas to persons and companies, reviewed CCTV footage and examined documents linked to the attempt to transport large quantities of illegal drugs using chartered aircraft. – Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Health promotion budget cut flagged
articles.summary: Former Department of Health secretaries have expressed alarm over the drastic budget cut to the DOH Health Promotion Bureau, warning lawmakers that it is a violation of the Universal Health Care Act.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am

From the proposed P2.5 billion, the HPB’s 2027 budget has been reduced to P485 million, or 0.18 percent of the DOH’s total budget, in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 general appropriations bill.
BW FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — Former Department of Health secretaries have expressed alarm over the drastic budget cut to the DOH Health Promotion Bureau, warning lawmakers that it is a violation of the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act.

Section 30 of the UHC Law states that “the cost of implementing health promotion programs shall be at least one percent of the DOH’s total budget appropriations, ” the Healthy Philippines Alliance (HPA) stressed.

“Slashing funding for the prevention of noncommunicable diseases will ultimately cost the government far more in secondary care and emergency hospitalizations in the future,” said Jaime Galvez Tan, former health secretary and HPA lead convener.

“Diabetes, heart and kidney disease and hypertension are overwhelming Filipino families and draining our health care system. Prevention is our most cost-effective tool and we urge Congress to restore and expand funding to protect public health,” he added.

Filipino families, especially those from low-income households, lose the support and resources they need to protect them from preventable risks when the budget for health promotion shrinks to P400 million, former health secretary Esperanza Cabral said.
“It strips the poor of their right to services that can save their lives. We cannot protect vulnerable communities when HPB is severely underfunded,” Cabral said.

Former health secretary Manuel Dayrit said, “A budget cut of this scale undermines the mandate of the UHC Law. It is counterproductive to our goal of achieving a financially sustainable universal health care, which is fundamentally guaranteed to every Filipino.”

articles.title: PNP probing escape of Atong Ang

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is investigating how fugitive businessman Charlie “Atong” Ang managed to elude law enforcement authorities and leave the country.

Ang, the alleged mastermind in the kidnapping and killing of cockfighting aficionados or sabungeros, has fled the Philippines and is reportedly in Cambodia, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla.
PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said there is an ongoing probe on Ang’s reported departure in coordination with other concerned government agencies.
“We will be investigating all circumstances surrounding this development,” he said at a news briefing in Camp Crame in Quezon City.

articles.title: DepEd eyes data-driven criteria to solve classroom shortages
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) will be including data-driven criteria to determine and prioritize areas with the most severe classroom shortages.

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am
In a statement yesterday, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said classroom allocations must be responsive to school needs and directed toward areas facing the most severe shortages.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will be including data-driven criteria to determine and prioritize areas with the most severe classroom shortages.

Angara made this assurance after the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) issued a report on gaps in allocations for local government units (LGUs) with the highest estimated shortages, based on initial 2026 allocations.
DepEd stressed that allocation decisions will continue to weigh the severity of shortages, site readiness, project feasibility and implementation timelines.

Angara explained that in order to accelerate infrastructure delivery, DepEd is deploying a multi-pronged strategy that integrates Department of Public Works and Highways-led construction, LGU partnerships, public-private partnerships, DepEd Learning Continuity Spaces and collaborative initiatives with both government and private sector organizations.
Under the current LGU-led classroom construction initiative, allocations cover 439 LGUs, 1,955 schools and 8,777 classrooms nationwide.
Complementing these efforts, DepEd’s tripartite agreements with the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. and 48 LGUs have so far secured 576 classrooms for construction in priority communities.

To strengthen transparency and accountability, DepEd maintains oversight through regular physical and financial progress reporting, technical validation and monitoring protocols across division, regional and central office levels.

articles.title: DPWH: Government pursuing full restitution vs errant flood contractors
articles.summary: The national government is actively pursuing full monetary restitution and criminal accountability against rogue contractors involved in the multibillion-peso flood control scandal, according to…

blocks.text: October 23, 2026 | 12:00am
Department of Public Works and Highways.
Businessworld / File

MANILA, Philippines — The national government is actively pursuing full monetary restitution and criminal accountability against rogue contractors involved in the multibillion-peso flood control scandal, according to Secretary Vince Dizon of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

Responding to queries during an inspection of ongoing dike repairs in Calumpit, Bulacan last Wednesday, Dizon assured the public that the government has not written off the public funds lost to substandard, overpriced infrastructure projects previously executed by controversial firms like those owned by private contractor couple Curlee and Sarah Discaya as well as Wawao Builders.

“The legal process is moving forward,” Dizon said. “Government agencies, including the Office of the Ombudsman, the Office of the Solicitor General and the Department of Justice, are handling the cases. Most of the personalities involved are already detained, while authorities continue to track down remaining fugitives.”

Dizon emphasized that the prosecution strategy includes forcing errant contractors to reimburse the full cost of defective and unfinished flood control assets under the legal doctrine of restitution championed by the ombudsman.

“It is not enough that they are behind bars; they must return every peso stolen from the public,” he said. “While the justice system handles the recovery and prosecution, the DPWH’s job today is to fix the flood defenses in Calumpit and ensure that future projects are built correctly and transparently.”

articles.title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
articles.summary: Raghad and Raad's family had to flee their home on foot because of the fighting between pro-government forces and the Houthis.

blocks.text: Watch: Children in Yemen face homelessness and malnutrition as war rages
ByOrla Guerin
Senior International CorrespondentReporting fromAden
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.
They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.

When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.
What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.

"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden

blocks.text: The twins' family walked for three days before being given a lift to Aden
As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.
Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.
The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says

blocks.text: More than 250,000 people have been displaced over the past three months, the UN says
Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.
The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.
Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.
The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.
The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.
Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina

blocks.text: Raad was unable to keep down the fortified milk he was fed by his mother Lina

We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.
"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."
Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.
"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."
Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.

Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition

blocks.text: Raghad, like her brother, was diagnosed as having severe acute malnutrition
As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.
There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.
That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.
"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.
"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."
A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.
Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment

blocks.text: Dr Noor Mohammed says families with no money or insurance depend on her hospital for treatment
The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.
"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."
They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.
"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."
She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street

blocks.text: Bajash and his other children were forced to sleep on the street
Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.

As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.
So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi

articles.title: Macron bans ‘illegitimate‘ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
articles.summary: French president will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ regarding demonstrations on Friday as part of tough security response to recent rioting

blocks.text: Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.

Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.

Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but may have to use alternative routes.

The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”

blocks.caption: Macron attended the security council meeting at the Élysée Palace on Thursday as he sought to restore calm. Photograph: Suarez Teresa/ABACA/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the Republic”.

“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was later overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for that day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.
after newsletter promotion

Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of the Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.

Authorities in Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.

However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.

blocks.caption: A demonstration involving members of the gilets jaunes on the capital’s Place de la Republique on Saturday. Photograph: Giulia Morici/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big city mayors later in the day.

The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Elysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.

The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections that will choose Macron’s successor.

articles.title: Rogers to charge new fee for bills paid by credit card, says practice is ‘increasingly common’
articles.summary: Rogers Communications says a new 1.6 per cent “credit card processing charge” will apply starting Jan. 17.

image.caption: Rogers Communications is introducing a fee in January for customers who pay their bill by credit card. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New
Rogers Communications says a new 1.6 per cent “credit card processing charge” will apply starting Jan. 17.
Rival telecom firm Telus rolled out similar fee in 2022, before scrapping it a year later
Rogers Communications says it will roll out a new fee early next year for customers who pay their bill with a credit card.
The Canadian telecom giant says a 1.6 per cent “credit card processing charge” will apply starting Jan. 17. The company says this will impact both auto-pay and one-time credit card payments.
“The charge applies every time you pay your Rogers bill with a credit card,” Rogers says on its website.
“This reflects the fees we are charged by credit card companies.”
Rogers adds 1.6% surcharge for credit card payments | Hanomansing Tonight

According to Rogers, the fee is not applicable to customers in Quebec, as well as those on certain “specialized plans,” or former Shaw Mobile customers who migrated to Rogers when it acquired Shaw Communications in 2023.
Other forms of payment are not subject to the new fee. These include direct debt and online banking payments, cheques, Rogers gift cards, prepaid cards, Debit Mastercard and Visa Debit.
“If you choose to pay your bill by credit card, it's increasingly common across many sectors for a credit card fee to apply,” Rogers said.
Telus scrapped similar fee

In 2022, rival telecom provider Telus asked the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) for permission to add a 1.5 per cent surcharge to the bills of some landline phone customers who pay their bill using a credit card. The CRTC rejected this request.
However, the regulator’s approval was only required for a fee on landline services. Telus rolled out a 1.5 per cent credit card fee for mobile and home internet customers.
Telus scrapped the fee in 2023, following a settlement between credit card companies and merchants allowing merchants to pass on the cost directly to customers.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron
articles.summary: Some cities including Lyon and Nice have banned all protests, and the French president said only authorised demos would be allowed.

blocks.text: Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.

Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.
Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.

"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.

"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement.
Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.

Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests.

Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the office, housed in a 19th-Century building, was "a tragedy".
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la République was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
Following the unrest, France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez tendered his resignation, which was rejected by President Macron.
The Élysée Palace asked him instead to look at how to make France's streets safer and bring rioters to justice.
Nuñez said his teams had forecast 200,000 demonstrators, a figure much lower than the 550,000 estimated to have gathered.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla on Thursday said that his office will review the evidence that the House prosecution will turn over from the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

After the House prosecution panel dropped three of the four articles of impeachment against Duterte, lead prosecutor Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville “Jinky” Luistro said that the prosecution team was ready to turn over any evidence to the Ombudsman if needed.
“Probably we will be needing sworn statements. We will evaluate it first. And we will see if we need sworn statements to come with the relay of information,” Remulla said in a press briefing in Cebu.

After presenting three articles of impeachment—Article IV on grave threats, Article I on confidential funds use, and Article II on unexplained wealth—the House prosecution panel withdrew the articles on grave threats and confidential funds. Luistro said that the evidence and testimonies presented in arguing these articles will not be wasted.

“As part of our appeal to the public, huwag po tayong manghinayang because these articles are not gone into waste sapagkat tuloy-tuloy po ang ibang ahensya ng ating pamahalaan to pursue criminal action with respect to these articles of impeachment,” Luistro said.

(As part of our appeal to the public, we urge you not to feel dismayed because these articles are not gone into waste as other agencies of the government will continue to pursue criminal action with respect to these articles of impeachment.)
Asked about the National Bureau of Investigation’s (NBI) probe into Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), Remulla said that it needed to be validated first.
“Fact-finding muna yan [Fact-finding first]. So this is a process where we validate the facts that are being presented to us,” Remulla said.

articles.title: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France
articles.summary:
Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death

A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus,…

blocks.text: A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.

Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety, in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”.
“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.

The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection.
It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.
“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said.

Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low. “Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.
“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”

But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.

“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing. This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”
Dr Ben Brennan from the MRC-University of Glasgow’s centre for virus research, said there was currently no evidence of sustained transmission between humans.

“While this discovery warrants further scientific investigation and continued surveillance, it does not currently suggest a significant new public health threat to the UK,” he said. “For most people, there is no reason to change their normal activities or take additional precautions.”

articles.title: 2027 budget has no unconstitutional items, says DBM
articles.summary: The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Thursday told senators that the provisions that the Supreme Court (SC) declared unconstitutional in the 2024 and 2025 budgets were no longer in the…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 11:01pm

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Thursday told senators that the provisions that the Supreme Court (SC) declared unconstitutional in the 2024 and 2025 budgets were no longer in the proposed 2027 budget.

In a "24 Oras" report from Mav Gonzales, senators questioned DBM Secretary Kim De Leon about what adjustments needed to be made following the SC order to ensure that there were no constitutional infirmities.

“We don't have SAGIP (Strengthening Assistance for Government Infrastructure and Social Programs) anymore even in 2027 Unprogrammed Appropriations (UA). The Supreme Court has also laid down some guardrails, the four guardrails to make the unprogrammed appropriations constitutional. Among these is that there shouldn’t be any lump sum,” De Leon said.

The SAGIP items in the UA of both the 2024 and 2025 national budgets were deemed illegal by the SC, as it gave the executive branch post-enactment identification or allocative powers — a duty only prescribed to Congress.
The UA is a list of projects that do not have a set allotment of money for them unless government revenues meet or surpass its targets.

In 2024, the executive branch asked Congress for P281 billion in UA funds, but Congress increased it to P731 billion. The following year, Congress again increased the UA from P158 billion to P363 billion.
The 2026 budget also has a UA, but this no longer surpassed what the President asked for.
The proposed 2027 budget still has UA, but this is the lowest since 2019.

“Bottom line… hindi pwede lumampas Kongreso sa proposal ng Presidente both unprogrammed and programmed?” Senate President Win Gatchalian asked. (Bottom line… Congress could not surpass what was proposed by the President both unprogrammed and programmed?)
“That is how we view the decision, your honor,” De Leon replied.
The DBM will also not release funding from Sections 1A and 1B of the 2026 budget if the government does not surpass its revenue targets. Unless the funding is for foreign-assisted projects (FAP),
No UA will also be released from the 2024 budget because this has expired, while the P17.99 billion from the 2025 UA remained untouched.
Senator Imee Marcos said that the obligations for the FAP must be paid.

“We’d like to assure the good senator and the committee na wala pong tatalbog na tseke for foreign-assisted projects, dahil ito ay under a direct financing scheme. Direktang pong binabayaran ng development funders, development institutions, ang ating contractors,” De Leon said.

(We’d like to assure the good senator and the committee that no cheques will bounce for foreign-assisted projects, because this is under a direct financing scheme. We are directly paying the development funders, development institutions, and our contractors.)

Senator Francis Pangilinan said that the previous budgets need not be worried about, and it will only apply moving forward, citing a conversation with SC Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, who penned the decision.
“He actually said that as far as 2024 and 2025 are concerned, the doctrine of post-operative fact will apply,” Pangilinan said.—Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
articles.summary:
‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by…

blocks.text: When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.

But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.

This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.

“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”

The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.

The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.

The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.

Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”

Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.

Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.

“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”

For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.

Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”

The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.

Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.

“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.
“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”
Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.

“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”

During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.
For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.

“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

articles.title: Ron Duguay, hockey star who made impact on and off ice, dead at 69
articles.summary: Ron Duguay, who starred for his hometown Sudbury Wolves and became an immediate sensation on and off the ice with the New York Rangers, has died. He was 69.

image.caption: Ron Duguay, right, is shown in New York City on Feb. 21, 2020 at a charitable event for Ronald McDonald House New York. Duguay, most synonymous with the New York Rangers in a 12-year NHL career, died Thursday. (Monica Schipper/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Ron Duguay, who starred for his hometown Sudbury Wolves and became an immediate sensation on and off the ice with the New York Rangers, has died. He was 69.
Duguay represented Canada, reached Stanley Cup final while fielding plenty of endorsements
Ron Duguay, who starred for his hometown Sudbury Wolves and became an immediate sensation on and off the ice in the Big Apple with the New York Rangers, has died. He was 69.
Shay Thomas, Duguay's daughter, said in post shared with her two siblings and Duguay's partner that the 12-year NHL player died Thursday "after a hard fought battle with cancer."
"Our hearts are broken. We love you forever Dad," said Thomas, who added that a celebration of life would be announced at a future date.

Sarah Palin, the former Alaska governor and 2008 vice-presidential candidate who was Duguay's girlfriend for at least the past four years, posted a bedside picture on social media on Oct. 18 holding his hand. "Prayers for Ron Duguay so appreciated," she said.

Duguay told the New York Post in February that he had had Stage 4 cancer for about a year at that time, which had originated in the colon. Duguay's daughters Shay and Amber from his first marriage had started a GoFundMe to help their father fund treatment, which involved travelling to California from his Florida home.

Duguay appears with Mark Carney, then the Bank of England governor, at Trafalgar Square, London, for a 'Canada 150' celebration, on July 1, 2017. Janice Charette, then Canada's high commissioner to Britain, is also shown. (Matt Dunham/The Associated Press)

The Wolves held a Ron Duguay Appreciation Night on Sept. 30 to help with his health-care expenses. Wayne Gretzky, in a video message for the event, said he was pulling for the man who was his Canada Cup teammate in 1981 as well as with the Los Angeles Kings later that decade. Gretzky called Duguay a "great person, great family guy."

In a career that also saw him play with legends Phil Esposito, Steve Yzerman and Mario Lemieux, Duguay notched 274 goals and 346 assists for 620 points in 860 NHL games over a dozen seasons. The totals were impressive enough, but in an era when hockey players often didn't make an impression beyond the game's hardcore fans, he was an exception, his smooth skating and helmet-less long, curly locks providing an indelible image in the sport in the late 1970s and early '80s.
Off-ice sensation

Duguay was featured in a cover story in Andy Warhol's Interview magazine, was regularly admitted beyond the velvet rope at Manhattan's legendary Studio 54 nightclub, where Liza Minnelli introduced herself and later connected him with Cher, who he would date for a time.

He was signed by Elite Models for promotional appearances, appeared in a hilarious and now-cringey chorus-line style ad with three Rangers teammates to promote Vidal Sassoon jeans, and partnered with Esposito and teammate Ron Greschner in a Manhattan bar called Sticks.
Duguay, then with the New York Rangers, poses for a portrait on the streets on Manhattan in March 1980. (Bruce Bennett Studios/Getty Images)

Duguay, in large part, backed up the hype off the ice with his play. Drafted 13th overall by the Rangers in 1977, made the jump to the NHL without playing a single game in the minor leagues. The six-foot-two, 210-pound player would earn the respect of his NHL foes as a two-way player.

"When he's on, he's a dominant force," Craig Ramsay of the Buffalo Sabres said in a 1980 feature for the Toronto Star. "You can't believe how much ice he covers killing penalties, and he's always a scoring threat on the power play."

Duguay, born to parents Fern and Anita on July 6, 1957, grew up in northern Ontario, delivering newspapers for the Sudbury Star and gaining strength as a teenager as his father was an avid weightlifter.

He would average 33 goals and 90 points with the Wolves over four seasons in Sudbury, eventually becoming team captain, in what was then called the Ontario Hockey Association (OHA). He represented Canada at the first official world junior hockey championship in 1977, when the team won silver.
Duguay had been mandated to wear a helmet like all OHA players, but chose not to wear one in the NHL. After having his head shaved in an initiation ritual as a rookie, he grew his hair back.
Duguay and Robin Bobo are seen together on Sept. 9, 1983, a few months before their marriage. (Mary Schroeder/Imagn Images/USA Today Network/Reuters)

New York had missed the playoffs in the previous two seasons but made the postseason in his rookie year as he successfully switched from centre to right wing. In his second season, talented Swedes Anders Hedberg and Ulf Nilsson joined the team after playing for Winnipeg in the World Hockey Association, and the Rangers would make the Stanley Cup final before falling to the Montreal Canadiens. Duguay earned nine points in 18 playoff games during that run.

They were heady days for the Rangers. The team also featured Don Murdoch, the talented forward who was once suspended for half the season after beinag caught with five grams of cocaine at the U.S.-Canada border.
Duguay admitted decades later in a podcast that he palled off-ice with Murdoch and sometimes made it to practice without having had any sleep.
"We would do things to keep us awake," he joked.
Canada Cup appearance

After a 40-goal season with the Rangers in 1980-81, Duguay was invited to camp for the 1981 Canada Cup tournament and impressed coach Scotty Bowman and the staff enough to land a spot. Duguay would appear in all seven games as Canada lost to the Soviet Union in the final, and he remembered it decades later in an interview with the Saint-John Telegraph Journal as likely his proudest achievement as a pro player.

Things soured in the 1982-83 NHL season with the Rangers, when he notched just 19 goals. The famed coach Herb Brooks questioned his commitment on the ice and Sonny Werblin, chair of Madison Square Garden, called him a "big, big disappointment."
Duguay, left, plays for the Los Angeles Kings in 1988-89, toward the end of his NHL career. (Mike Powell/Allsport/Getty Images)

Duguay admitted to a reporter days after being traded to then-lowly Detroit in June 1983 that he was depressed about the move, but he would recover to record 80 and 89 points in his first two seasons with the Red Wings, the highest totals of his NHL career.

In December 1983, the New York Daily News reported on his marriage to American model Robin Bobo, writing that Duguay was "finally taking the plunge after being a free agent with such beauties as Cheryl Tiegs etc. etc."

Beginning with a trade to the Penguins late in the 1985-86 season, Duguay would have relatively short stints with Pittsburgh, the Rangers again and in Los Angeles. By the 1990s, he was playing in Germany and in the minor leagues in San Diego.
Duguay's first marriage eventually ended, and in 1994 he would welcome a son, Noah, with his second wife, the model Kim Alexis.

Duguay and Sarah Palin appear together during a campaign event on July 9, 2022, in Anchorage, when she was in the middle of an unsuccessful run for a U.S. Congress seat. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Duguay stayed busy in retirement. He appeared on an episode of Beverly Hills 90210, coached the Jacksonville Barracudas in the minor leagues for four seasons, spent time as a commentator for the Rangers on the Madison Square Garden network and participated in the first season of CBC's Battle of the Blades with Olympian Barbara Underhill.

Duguay told the Eddie Matta Show podcast in 2021 that he had been single for about seven years, but reports of the Duguay-Palin relationship emerged the following year. She would initially describe him as a "buddy," but he would be by her side as she launched an unsuccessful bid for Congress and was embroiled in a defamation lawsuit with the New York Times.

articles.title: Canadian high diver welcomed fear during historic leap off Newfoundland iceberg
articles.summary: In the last year, Canada's Molly Carlson has jumped from a moving helicopter into a cage surrounded by sharks, completed her highest dive yet from a 27-metre platform, and, in her latest…

image.caption: High diver Molly Carlson of Thunder Bay, Ont., says she was keen to take on a challenge that showcased natural Canada and was partly inspired from watching fellow high diver Orlando Duque, who dove off an iceberg in Antarctica in 2018. (Handout/YouTube/Red Bull/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: In the last year, Canada's Molly Carlson has jumped from a moving helicopter into a cage surrounded by sharks, completed her highest dive yet from a 27-metre platform, and, in her latest nerve-defying feat, became the first woman to dive off an iceberg.
Battling intrusive thoughts, she leapt from edge, soon feeling bliss in 'dive of my dreams'

In the last year, Molly Carlson has jumped from a moving helicopter into a cage surrounded by sharks, completed her highest dive yet from a 27-metre platform, and, in her latest nerve-defying feat, became the first woman to dive off an iceberg.
Yet, the Canadian high diver will be the first person to tell you she's not, in fact, fearless.
“I don't feel like I've ever conquered fear,” Carlson said. “I've just learned more about it, and I've welcomed it and I have grown with it.”

Carlson lives with fear every day as one of the world’s best in the extreme sport of cliff diving, where she leaps off 21m platforms and performs acrobatics while reaching speeds up to 85 km/h in the air, before landing feet first in the water.

The 28-year-old from Thunder Bay, Ont., is also an influencer with a following of more than eight million across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, where she built an online community, and company, known as Brave Gang that celebrates all forms of bravery and self-love.
Carlson has shared much of her athletic and personal journey through social media, including her historic iceberg dive, documented in the short film "Red Bull Iceberg Dive," available on YouTube.

The 30-minute documentary details Carlson's preparation for the stunt, including cold-water training and learning to ice climb from fellow Canadian Red Bull athlete Will Gadd, whose accomplishments include ascending a frozen wall on the American side of Niagara Falls. Six months of training led to the moment in June, when Carlson climbed and dove off an estimated 14m iceberg off the coast of Newfoundland into 1 C water.

Carlson said she was keen to take on a challenge that highlighted natural Canada and was partly inspired from watching fellow high diver Orlando Duque, who dove off an iceberg in Antarctica in 2018. From conception to execution, Carlson said the project was about four years in the making.
Dealing with unknown stressful
And while Carlson is accustomed to competing in a high-risk sport, this endeavour presented unique danger.

Unlike a stationary platform or cliff, icebergs move and can roll over, which meant experts had to find what Carlson deemed the "unicorn" iceberg that was stable to scale and had a shelf to safely dive from. Dealing with the unknown of when, or if, the dive would happen was stressful on Carlson, who at one point becomes emotional about the toll it's taking in the documentary. Talking about the experience months later, Carlson said she was prepared to abort the plan if it couldn't be performed safely.

"If we get there, it's too dangerous, it's not the vibe, something feels off, we both have to be comfortable in our expertise to say no," she said of her discussion that included Gadd. "The whole time we were in Newfoundland, we didn't know until like 30 minutes before if it was even possible."

items: Canadian diver reflects on terrifying cliff fall, overcoming near-death experience
How Molly Carlson used empowering messages to help overcome mental health struggle

blocks.text: Even with the ideal iceberg, there were challenges. Carlson typically knows the exact height of the platform she dives from which is important in a calculated sport like diving. But the iceberg's height, measured by drones, wasn't precise, meaning she had to rely on her athletic instincts.
"I really had to use my eyes in the air to be able to adjust how fast or slow I go," she said. "It was really going to be, fix yourself in the air to land safely," she said.
Scaling the iceberg unnerved Carlson, too. Gadd set up a rope and guided her to the top, but still Carlson said, "This is not my expertise."
At the top, conditions were windy, and Carlson had to battle intrusive thoughts. But when she leapt from the iceberg's edge into her backflip, she felt "bliss."
"I felt like I was in the air for like 10 minutes," said Carlson, who landed without a splash, calling it "the dive of my dreams."
Cliff diver Molly Carlson talks about the importance of staying authentic
Relationship with fear has changed

Carlson, who has been open about living with anxiety and overcoming an eating disorder as a competitive teenage diver, said her relationship to fear has changed over the years. When she was in high school, she said, she thought she wasn't allowed to have anxious or negative feelings. But as an adult, she said, "I realized fear keeps you safe."

"If you can find the right balance of fear and welcome it into your life, you can actually find calm with it, versus putting so much energy and pressure to push it away, it's just going to distract you," she said. "As soon as I realized that, so much of my anxiety calmed down."

items: Carlson captures silver medal at 2024 World Aquatics Championships
More aquatics coverage

blocks.text: In the end, Carlson executed the iceberg dive exactly how she wanted, but she would have been happy with any outcome, she said.

"Before I welcomed fear, I bet I would have gone to that iceberg and been like, 'If you mess up this time, if you make a splash, I'm going to be so embarrassed.' And that's just so not the priority anymore," she said. "The priority is to go, to make a difference, to show people that you're allowed to be scared and do it anyways.
"That's the biggest message, and I think bravery comes from accepting that fear is allowed to be there," she said.
Most people cannot identify with Carlson's athletic or adventurous exploits, but she said she thinks being open about her anxiety makes her relatable.
"And to show that I'm still human up on these crazy heights," she said.

articles.title: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
articles.summary: After two years of student protests, Serbians vote on Sunday in elections that could bring down the ruling party.

blocks.text: Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
Image source, Reuters
Young Serbians have been the driving force behind the movement, but none of the candidates are students
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor
Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.
After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.
The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.
Why is this student movement so important?
They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.

The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The canopy over the front of the station in Novi Sad collapsed without warning on 1 November 2024

What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.

The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.

At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.
Who is Vučić and how popular is he?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that

blocks.text: Vučić has been prime minister or president since 2014, and was deputy prime minister for two years before that
Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.

Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".

Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power.

"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.
How do Serbia's elections work?
Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.
Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.
There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.
Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.
Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.
Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for?

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates

blocks.text: Ilija Srdanović (in yellow) tops the list of Student List candidates
Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.

They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić.
Under an 11-point programme, external, the student movement wants to:

items: eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it
purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime
reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control
stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises

blocks.text: Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
How fair will the vote be?

European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".

Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence, external, and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.
In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".

Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".
Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year, says the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom.

articles.title: SWS: 42% of Filipinos follow Sara Duterte's impeachment trial closely
articles.summary: Less than half of Filipinos follow the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte either closely or somewhat closely, according to the Social Weather Stations (SWS).

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 10:22pm
Less than half of Filipinos follow the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte either closely or somewhat closely, according to the Social Weather Stations (SWS).
Broken down further, 15% followed the trial very closely, 28% followed it somewhat closely, 21% followed it just a little, and 27% did not follow it at all.
The SWS said there were 9% of respondents who only heard about the impeachment trial during the interview.

The survey was taken from September 21 to 27, before the House prosecution panel dropped three out of the four impeachment articles. At the time, the House prosecution was presenting evidence on Article II or the unexplained wealth. This is the only article that the panel did not drop.
According to the SWS, fewer people followed Duterte’s impeachment when compared to former president Joseph Estrada and the late Chief Justice Renato Corona.
For Estrada’s impeachment, 47% followed it very or somewhat closely. For Corona, 52% to 54% followed his impeachment, according to two separate SWS polls.
The SWS made use of face-to-face interviews of 1,500 adults, with 600 of them in Balance Luzon, and 300 each in Metro Manila, Visayas and Mindanao. The sampling error for national percentages is ±3%.
Around 38% of respondents discussed the trial with their families, with 4% always discussing it, 9% often, and 25% sometimes. Then there were 37% who rarely discussed it and 26% who never did.

Half of the respondents said the trial gave the right consideration to both sides. The SWS said 18% of Filipinos found that the trial was too liberal with Duterte’s defense team, and 17% said that it was too liberal with prosecutors. There was 15% who did not give an opinion.
In terms of the trial’s pacing, the SWS said that 39% of respondents said the trial was too slow, 31% said it was just the right pace, and 22% said they were in too much of a hurry.

Asked about whether or not they trusted the Senate to make a fair decision in Duterte’s case, 28% said they had much trust, 32% were undecided, and 35% had little trust, resulting in a net trust score of -7.
Net trust scores for both Estrada and Corona’s trial were higher, but used different scales than the one used in Duterte’s survey. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Is Iran ready for another major US attack after midterm elections?
articles.summary: Tehran has said its goal is to keep the regime functioning and threaten enough regional costs to make a prolonged campaign unattractive. US media reports indicate Washington is considering strikes…

image.caption: The US currently has 2 aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East, with a third on the way [FILE: 2019]Image: Zachary Pearson/US Navy/AFP

blocks.text: The prospect of another major US attack is shaping calculations in Tehran, where officials are preparing for renewed strikes.
According to US media reports, the US and Israel have been examining new options for strikes against Iran.

The approaching US midterm elections on November 3, and Israel's election next week, have injected a political factor into how both countries are approaching the conflict they launched in late February.

Polls show high energy prices brought on by the Iran war are hurting Trump's Republicans. On October 8, Trump posted on social media that the US would not attack Iran before the midterms, citing "productive discussions" with Tehran. The US last launched strikes on Iran in early September.
However, after the elections are over, Trump may feel less politically constrained in launching attacks on Iran.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, meanwhile, has campaigned on a platform of regime change in Tehran.

blocks.caption: Analysts say Iran's regime is preparing to crack down on unrest unleashed by possible US strikes [FILE: 2022]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Report says plans in place for 'short' US-Israeli operation

On Wednesday, the New York Times, citing senior US officials, reported that the US and Israel have "developed specific plans" for a "short but intensive operation" in Iran that would include targets like Iran's nuclear facilities, energy infrastructure, and arsenal of missiles and drones.

One official told the newspaper the goal would be to force Iran into making "diplomatic concessions" by further weakening its economy, as negotiations to end the conflict have gone nowhere. The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz that has sapped Tehran's oil revenues.

The Times report follows others in recent weeks, including Axios in early October, which reported that the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command "to conclude preparations for resuming major combat operations in Iran."
There are currently two US aircraft carrier strike groups in the Arabian Sea, with a third expected to arrive by late November.

On October 15, Trump told the right-wing broadcaster Newsmax that he was considering a strike on Pickaxe Mountain near the Natanz nuclear complex, where US officials believe Iran may have moved sensitive nuclear-related material underground.

A day later, CNN reported Trump was considering using a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, on Iranian targets. As the MOAB creates a massive blast wave above ground, its effectiveness in targeting underground facilities like Pickaxe would be limited.
Iran says it has learned from earlier attacks
Iranian officials, meanwhile, have said they are prepared for another US attack, with a broad response that would include regional US bases and energy facilities in the Gulf.

Ali Asghar Shafieian, a media adviser to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, told DW that although the US retains a significant technological and military advantage, Tehran's strategy is based on preserving the regime's hold on the country, rather than matching US strength.
"The United States has the upper hand in military power and technology, but Iran's strength is in how it deals with a crisis," Shafieian said.

He pointed to the rapid replacement of senior officials killed in previous attacks as an example of how Tehran has tried to make its political structure more resilient. Iran has also been rebuilding its missile and drone capabilities that were hit during the massive wave of strikes seen during the first weeks of the war.

Reuters news agency, citing Iranian officials, reported this week that Iran is "preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war," adding that Tehran was prolonging negotiations to try and weaken Trump ahead of the midterms.
Tehran has told regional governments that US military bases and critical infrastructure could become targets if neighboring countries assist another US or Israeli operation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that participation or cooperation by regional states would face what he called a "decisive and proportionate response."

"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust and reach a just solution. But if the US "chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure," Araghchi posted on X.
US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran?
How is Iran preparing for new strikes?
Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based political analyst, told DW Iran's preparations extend beyond missiles and drones into prioritizing internal security.
That includes confronting armed opposition groups, preparing for possible protests and developing plans to prevent external military pressure from combining with domestic unrest.
Another conflict, he said, could bring renewed internet restrictions and a stronger mobilization of government supporters in public spaces.
"In the government's asymmetric-war strategy, the ultimate objective is to convince the United States that regime change through military action is impossible," Ghahremanpour said.

Ghahremanpour added that some factions within Iran have supported returning to a negotiated agreement. But he believes Washington's demands are now considered so extensive that even Iranian officials favoring compromise struggle to build domestic support for them.
"For now, we are facing a deadlock," he said. "Iranian officials do not appear optimistic about reaching an agreement."
Talks continue to stall over Iran's nuclear program, which US officials say must top the agenda.

Iran's latest proposal to the US, sent through Qatari mediators, included an offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under Iranian control, in exchange for Washington lifting its maritime blockade, releasing frozen assets and ending military actions.

A report this week from the Wall Street Journal, citing data from ship tracker Kpler, shows that oil flows through Hormuz are approaching pre-war levels as the US military escorts tankers and shipping companies are more willing to take risks for a bigger payoff. This raises questions about Tehran's weakening leverage over oil flows.
Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal is reached
Fear of war inside Iran
For ordinary Iranians, another confrontation would come amid severe economic pressure and growing political polarization.
A female doctor in Tehran told DW that she fears what will happen if fighting returns. Speaking with the media in Iran remains very dangerous, and she spoke under condition of anonymity.
"The economic situation has become extremely bad," she said. "Even if you have a good income yourself, you don't feel good living among so many people struggling with poverty," she added.
She expects authorities to restrict internet access again if fighting begins.
Another woman in Tehran described anger toward regime supporters and said another war combined with domestic protests could increase the risk of confrontations on the streets.
Asked about possible attacks on underground nuclear sites, she said the issue felt increasingly detached from her everyday problems.
"What do the nuclear sites have to do with us? They are inside mountains," she said.
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers
Edited: Emmy Sasipornkarn
