articles.title: Minister giving Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs before taking case to court

image.caption: Stelco's steel production facility in Hamilton is pictured from across the Hamilton Harbour in Burlington, Ont., on Oct. 9. (Nick Iwanyshyn/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is giving the American parent company of Hamilton-based Stelco 15 days to reverse layoffs before seeking legal action.
Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs says up to 500 temporary layoffs are due to U.S. tariffs
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is giving the American parent company of Hamilton-based Stelco 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts.
In a "demand letter" sent to Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs on Thursday, Joly says the company is violating its commitments under the Investment Canada Act.
"In the event Cliffs fails to comply with this demand, the Minister may, pursuant to section 40 of the Act, make an application to a superior court," the letter, obtained by Radio-Canada, reads.

Joly indicates that if the government proceeds with legal action, it would be asking the courts to issue monetary penalties against Cleveland-Cliffs and potentially direct the company to divest from Stelco.

"I remain prepared to sit down with Cleveland-Cliffs to find a solution. But our bottom line is clear: protect Canadian jobs, defend our steel industry and ensure that commitments made to Canada are respected," Joly said in a statement.
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly answers questions from reporters in Ottawa on Oct. 14. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Cleveland-Cliffs said late last month that it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles certain steel production at Stelco, a move the federal government says violates "binding commitments" made when it bought the company in 2024.

The federal government has said the company's purchase of Stelco included promises to employ "at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees" as there were in 2024 through 2029.
The company said the planned layoffs are in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs on steel squeeze its sales. But Joly has dismissed that reasoning.
"Let me be clear: no act of God or change in market conditions can relieve Cleveland-Cliffs of the commitments it made to Canada. Those commitments are not optional," she said in her statement.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Christian Noël

articles.title: Is EU putting profits over human rights in Vietnam?
articles.summary: The EU and Vietnam are deepening economic and diplomatic ties, but closer cooperation raises concerns about whether Brussels is doing enough to address Hanoi's human rights record, labor standards…

image.caption: Trade in goods between Vietnam and the EU reached €76 billion in 2025Image: Omar Havana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Vietnam's Communist Party chief and president, To Lam, arrived in Brussels on Wednesday for an official visit to the European Union (EU) and Belgium in another sign that relations continue to expand.
The visit comes just days after Vietnam signed a free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Trade ties between Vietnam and Europe have deepened in recent years. The EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), which took effect in August 2020, substantially expanded Vietnam's commercial ties with most European states.

Amid global tariff wars, the EU-Vietnam relationship "is a welcome advertisement for keeping markets open," Khac Giang Nguyen, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS–Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, told DW.

"This is a win-win for both sides," he said. "Vietnam offers Europe an established manufacturing base and another foothold in Asian supply chains. Europe offers Vietnam capital, technology and a large market, helping Hanoi reduce its exposure to American demand and Chinese industrial inputs."
Vietnam-EU ties deepen
Vietnam is now the EU's largest goods-trading partner in Southeast Asia and its 14th-largest globally. The EU is Vietnam's fourth-largest trading partner and a major source of foreign investment.
Noneconomic relations are also advancing. In January, both sides upgraded ties to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership — the first such agreement between the EU and a Southeast Asian country.
Vietnam has become a key strategic partner for the EU in the Indo-Pacific, Alfred Gerstl, an expert on Indo-Pacific international relations at the University of Vienna, told DW.

"The cooperation is crucial for advancing the EU's economic security agenda and its strategy of de-risking from China," he said, referring to the European Union's efforts to diversify its supply chains and reduce dependence on Chinese manufacturing.

Several EU states have signed defense agreements with Vietnam. Bloc foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas held talks with Vietnamese Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on Wednesday to discuss ways to improve security cooperation, including in the South China Sea, where Hanoi is locked in territorial disputes with China.
Concerns over Vietnam's human rights record

The relationship has also faced difficulties. Questions remain over whether European companies are benefiting sufficiently from Vietnam's economic boom and whether Brussels is overlooking Hanoi's worsening human rights record.

Vietnam remains a one-party communist state that severely restricts political opposition, independent journalism and civil society. Rights organizations say repression has intensified under To Lam, who previously headed the country's powerful public security ministry.

In an open letter sent this week to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa, 12 international human rights organizations raised "grave concerns over the Vietnamese government's intensifying repression" and urged EU leaders to demand meaningful reforms.
When negotiating the EVFTA and the accompanying political agreements, Hanoi agreed to obligations on human rights, labor protections and environmental standards.
These included commitments to reform labor legislation to permit independent worker organizations and align domestic regulations more closely with International Labour Organization (ILO) standards.
Rights groups say Hanoi has failed to deliver. Vietnam has still not ratified the ILO convention on freedom of association, and independent trade unions remain prohibited.
"The EU has taken no action in response to Vietnam's repeated breaches of its EVFTA-related obligations and pledges; instead, in January it upgraded bilateral relations," the joint letter read.

blocks.caption: Vietnam signed a free-trade agreement with four European countries — Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein — in Hanoi, on October, 18, 2026Image: Hoang Thong Nhat/Vietnam News Agency/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Benefits 'distributed unevenly'
There are also questions about which Vietnamese companies have benefited most from the EU's trade liberalization.

Large foreign-invested manufacturers and established exporters have been better placed to exploit tariff reductions than smaller domestic businesses, which often lack the resources to navigate Europe's complex import requirements.

Vietnamese exporters also face growing demands from the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and its deforestation regulations, which require businesses in affected sectors to provide more detailed information about their production processes and supply chains.

"It is quite clear that the EVFTA's benefits have been distributed unevenly across sectors, firms and social groups, while political, regulatory, and economic challenges may complicate the next phase of the relationship," Hai Thiem Bui, a researcher at the Stockholm Center for Global Asia, Stockholm University, told DW.

"The next phase of EU-Vietnam trade relations is likely to depend less on tariff liberalization and more on whether Vietnam can adapt to increasingly demanding EU standards concerning labor rights, sustainability, and regulatory governance," he added.
Better for EU?
Another challenge concerns how much European businesses are gaining from Vietnam's expanding export economy.
Although the EVFTA has considerably strengthened bilateral commerce, it has been far more successful at increasing Vietnamese exports to Europe than EU sales to Vietnam.
The EU's goods-trade deficit with Vietnam reached €51.7 billion ($57.9 billion) in 2025 — up from roughly €24 billion in 2019.
This imbalance is becoming more conspicuous as Brussels seeks greater economic security and new export opportunities for EU industries.
Is Vietnam set to replace China as the world's factory?
Another obstacle is the EU-Vietnam Investment Protection Agreement, signed in 2019, which has still not entered into force.

"We have also seen an uptick in investments by European businesses in Vietnam, despite the lack of an Investment Protection Agreement being in place," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
Germany ratified it in February and Poland followed in April, but France, the Netherlands and several other member states have yet to complete ratification.
The agreement will strengthen legal protections for investors and establish a permanent mechanism for resolving investment disputes, potentially encouraging greater EU investment in Vietnam.

"With a new government in Vietnam pursuing an ambitious legislative program but with an overall target of maintaining Vietnam's extraordinary growth path, we would expect trade to continue to flourish," Humphrey said.
"That said, many European businesses are looking carefully at what the legislative program may bring in terms of reform," he added.

For Brussels, the next phase of relations is about ensuring that EU businesses benefit from that growth, while demonstrating that its commitments to human rights and sustainable trade are more than diplomatic promises.

articles.title: Teacher in Oregon shooting said she pretended to be dead to survive
articles.summary: The teacher said she could not help children because she was badly injured by the attacker.

blocks.text: Some readers may find this article distressing.
A 54-year-old teacher who survived a mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school said she pretended to be dead so the gunman would not shoot her again.
Becky Drury, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, said in a statement shared with US media that as she tried to shut her classroom door, the gunman shot her and she fell to the floor.
"I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again," Drury said.
The attacker - who has been identified as a 16-year-old former student at the school - killed three students and a teacher before a parent from the school fatally shot him.

In her first remarks since the 15 October shooting in Bend, Oregon, Drury said that she went to see what was happening outside the special-education classroom, and after spotting the shooter, she tried to shut the door.
The attacker still managed to shoot her, so she could not help any of the children in the classroom.

"Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured," she said. "I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else."
Drury suffered serious but not life-threatening harm from the shooting, which killed five-year-old Rhoam Summer, an eight and eleven-year-old, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.
Police have said another teacher - who has not been named - attempted to disarm the gunman by throwing her mobile phone. She was not injured.
A father of two other children who had followed the suspect into the school then shot and killed the attacker, who officials named as Griffin J John II.
Reports had emerged that another teacher threw herself on top of a student to protect the child during the shooting, but Drury said she wanted to clear the record about what happened on 15 October.
"I know there has been contradictory reporting about my actions that day, but the truth is I was shot before I had any chance to act," she said in her statement.
Police have not yet shared a motive for the suspect, who officials say was a special-education needs student at Silver Rail.
Drury said what happened in the classroom was "unimaginable".
"[L]ike so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy," she said.

articles.title: YouTuber arrested after popular Indian finance influencer's suicide
articles.summary: V Harish, who ran the hugely popular Instagram account "Finance with Harish", was found dead on Tuesday.

blocks.text: A 27-year-old finance influencer's suicide in India has been mired in allegations of cyberbullying and started a conversation around who should give financial advice to investors.
V Harish - who ran a hugely popular Instagram account called "Finance with Harish" - was found dead on Tuesday morning at his home near Chennai, capital of the southern state of Tamil Nadu.
His suicide came just weeks after his account was disabled by Meta after complaints of irregularities.

In a complaint lodged with the police, his father J Vinayagam has alleged that his son took his life because of online harassment by Jason Samuel, a YouTuber and CEO of tech-centric venture studio Zemuria.
Police arrested Samuel on Thursday under suspicion of trying to "extort money from Harish" and posting "defamatory videos against him on social media".
BBC Tamil has not been able to reach him for comment. Earlier, he denier wrongdoing in a post on X.
The case has brought into focus the growing influence of financial content creators in India, where millions of first-time investors increasingly turn to social media for market advice.
Harish began posting videos about finance and investing around five years ago, building a substantial online following.

Over the years, he published more than 1,500 videos and amassed more than 1.3 million Instagram followers. He described himself as a financial adviser to "millionaires" and "high-net-worth individuals".
He often used music, film clips and photos of global political leaders to make dramatic videos while talking about the rise and fall of the share market and prices of gold and silver.

The videos, which broke down financial issues in simple terms, became hugely popular as they coincided with a rapid expansion in India's retail investor base, especially since the 2020 Covid-19 pandemic.
The country's largest stock exchange, the National Stock Exchange, said earlier this year it now had more than 130 million unique investors registered with it as opposed to under 30 million in 2019.

But in September, Meta took down Harish's Instagram page after receiving complaints he was not registered with Indian market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) - which is required under law to be able to offer investment advice or manage client portfolios.
A back-up account, which gained over 60,000 followers in a short time, was also subsequently taken down, external following complaints from social media users and others.
A few other accounts in his name remain on Instagram, though with much smaller followings - and it's not clear who runs them.
According to Harish's friends and family, he recorded a video message before his death in which he said that "five years of hard work has been stolen" from him, news channel NDTV reported, external.
The video, which has also been shared widely on social media, shows him speaking in Tamil and then switching to English to say "I'm very sorry" to his parents, sister, friends and followers.

Police say Harish's father J Vinayagam has blamed "cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his channels" for his son's suicide and named Jason Samuel in his complaint registered at Kanathur police station near Chennai.

Samuel had posted a video on his YouTube channel on 18 October questioning Harish's credentials since he did not have Sebi or Amfi (Association of Mutual Funds in India) registrations. In it, he mentioned that Harish's Instagram account had been disabled following complaints.
This, Vinayagam says, triggered severe online harassment and led to pressures that drove his son to take his own life.

"We demand that a proper investigation be conducted and legal action be taken against Jason Samuel and his accomplices, who spread defamation on social media and caused mental distress through cyberbullying," his complaint states.
A police statement says Vinayagam's complaint was registered under "abetment to suicide" and preliminary investigations found Samuel had a "role in this case".
"[Samuel] will be produced before court and sent to judicial custody," it says.
Samuel has defended the video in which he flagged Harish's lack of credentials saying he was acting in the consumer interest.
In a statement on X, Samuel said he was "deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life".
He however, rejected allegations of "cyber-bullying" Harish.
"I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of licence and authority, misrepresentation of licence and fraud... his illegal activity.
"I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper Sebi licence. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss," he wrote.

If you're having thoughts of suicide, or know someone that might be, you can find support lines in India via the AASRA website, external or globally via Befrienders Worldwide, external. In the UK you can call the Samaritans Helpline on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org, external.

articles.title: The great moth revival: how bogongs have bounced back
articles.summary:
This animated map shows the insect’s population exploding in Australia’s eastern states, with the endangered species coming back from the brink

If you live anywhere on the eastern side of…

blocks.text: If you live anywhere on the eastern side of Australia, you’ve probably noticed that bogong moths are back in a big way.

While we don’t yet have figures from ecologist-led surveys to compare with previous years, there is a wealth of data on the great moth revival being generated by citizen scientists across the eastern states.

In this animated map you can see bogong moth observations posted to the citizen science platform iNaturalist via the Bogong Watch project. Every dot is a sighting, which may include one or more moths.

blocks.caption: How Bogong Moths swarmed eastern Australia

blocks.text: While there are some caveats to keep in mind with citizen science data (observation numbers over time can be skewed because of differences in effort and participation, for example) it does clearly show how the moth population has exploded this year.
A rise from a great fall

Bogongs were once so common they numbered in the billions, according to researchers, with as many as 4 billion moths migrating to the Australian Alps in summer to aestivate in cool caves. The moths famously caused panic at the Sydney Olympics closing ceremony in 2000, and were known to invade Parliament House in Canberra each year.
But the bogong population declined slowly between 1980 and 2016, then crashed dramatically in the summer of 2017.

blocks.caption: Guardian graphic. Chart shows bogong moth abundance over decades, with recent years marked absent in red

blocks.text: Moth numbers were so low the species was described as “undetectable” in the alpine regions.

Ken Green, an ecologist who has been monitoring bogong moths for more than 40 years, previously told the Guardian that Australia’s drought through 2017, 2018 and 2019 was probably the largest contributor to the population crash, with pesticides and urban light pollution contributing to the slower decline from the 80s.

After those years of catastrophic decline, the explosion of bogongs across the skies of eastern Australia this spring is great news for the plants the moths pollinate and the endangered species that rely on them for food, including the mountain pygmy possum.

articles.title: Sexualised, violent threats: female Victorian MPs fear for their safety as they fight more than just next month’s election
articles.summary:
Hostility from constituents is not new for the state’s politicians, including its premiers. But the alleged attack on Helen Haines has sent a chill down the collective spine

  • Get our…

blocks.text: On Monday night, Georgie Purcell shared a statement on social media in support of Helen Haines, who earlier that day had been allegedly attacked by a constituent in her regional Victorian electorate.

Purcell, a Victorian upper house MP whose region partly overlaps with Haines’s federal electorate, wrote that the alleged attack had sent chills down her spine. Being a woman in politics, she said, had changed the way she moved through the world – where she parked her car, which route she took home, even whether she held public events at all.

It didn’t take long to receive validation of why her precautions were necessary: a constituent commented on her Haines statement, saying he wished it had happened to Purcell. Another, a little while later, said: “You should be scared.”
Purcell reported them both. Beyond that, she says, there is “nothing else she can do” as the threats lack the specificity police require to take further action.
It leaves her on “high alert” with just five weeks until the Victorian election.

“One thing that is on my mind is there is 10 days of prepoll approaching where anyone who does want to undertake a targeted attack on a candidate or a member of parliament, it won’t be hard to work out where they are,” she says.

Purcell is not alone. Nationals MP Annabelle Cleeland, whose electorate of Euroa covers 11,452 square kilometres, says, due to threats, she shares her live location with her husband and staff when on the road.
“I don’t feel like I signed up for this job to put my children in harm’s way and, right now, I’m frightened about that,” she told ABC Radio Melbourne on Thursday.
“It’s sexualised, it’s violent and they target your weaknesses and your vulnerabilities – your children, your home.”
MPs across Victoria’s political spectrum – predominantly women – have said that threats to their safety intensified during Victoria’s prolonged Covid lockdowns and have remained a constant since.

Few Victorians can forget that during the pandemic, an effigy of the then premier, Daniel Andrews, was subjected to a mock execution on the front steps of parliament amid debate over pandemic legislation.
The next day, Andrews said: “There are some people who are threatening me. They’re threatening my family. They are essentially attacking the safety of my family.”

It is understood the premier was receiving around-the-clock close personal protection at the time. During the 2022 election campaign, Andrews’ press conferences were largely kept out of public view. One exception, an event at a Caulfield dog park, drew a man intent on heckling him. In 2023, another man faced court on charges of stalking and harassing Andrews.
When he resigned in 2024, Andrews lost his security but remained as much a public figure. Just recently, images of where he has been living appeared on the front page of a national newspaper.

His successor, Jacinta Allan, also faced much hostility, particularly in regional Victoria, where communities opposed the government’s emergency services levy and laws that allow state body VicGrid and its contractors access to private land for transmission projects – without a landholder’s consent.

There was the 2025 Bush Summit – a day after the latter laws passed parliament – where, during her speech, Allan was relentlessly heckled, including by an audience member who stood on her chair with a noose around her neck. Allan’s staff left in tears.

On other occasions, cars believed to be carrying the premier have been blocked or followed, only for those inside found to be staff members or other ministers – including at a press conference during the January bushfires.
For six weeks a mobile billboard carrying the message “ditch the witch” and AI-generated images of Allan travelled around Melbourne’s CBD before being reported on.
Each incident generated footage that was widely shared by the media and on socials.
A former staff member of Allan’s said the former premier “legitimately feared for her safety”.
“She would say ‘Someone is going to be killed.’”
‘A turning point’
For the entire four years she has been in parliament, Purcell has received abuse, rape and death threats on social media over her positions on issues including duck hunting and racing.
But since beginning a relationship with federal Labor MP Josh Burns, Purcell has had access to more security measures – not because she is a Victorian MP, but because her partner is a federal one.

In Canberra, the Australian federal police manage threats against federal MPs, building up intelligence about repeated behaviour and patterns over time. In Victoria, Purcell says, individual complaints are dealt with separately by police.

blocks.caption: Victorian premier Ben Carroll (pictured) met on Wednesday with the Victorian electoral commissioner and the chief commissioner of police, as well as his cabinet, to discuss stronger safety measures for MPs. Photograph: Christoper Hopkins/AAP

blocks.text: With a state election looming, this may be about to change.

On Wednesday, the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, met with the Victorian electoral commissioner and the chief commissioner of police, Mike Bush, as well as his cabinet, to discuss stronger safety measures for MPs.

“This work will happen progressively and as soon as possible. What has happened must be a turning point for political debate in Victoria and around Australia. We must go forward with more respect and understanding of one another,” Carroll told reporters.
Earlier that morning, Bush said police were working to establish a centralised process for monitoring threats against MPs.
“We want a single-stop shop to report these things and have the ability to be very proactive,” he said.

As of Thursday afternoon, changes were yet to be communicated to Victorian MPs, who have been asked to attend a briefing with police on Friday. For now, their only guidance remains a Tuesday morning email from the Department of Parliamentary Services that advises them to monitor and control access to their electorate offices, check external areas on CCTV before leaving, and to remember that a duress button is available in an emergency.
It leaves MPs weighing the risk of being out in public with their constituents against the possibility that one may try to harm them.

items: Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

articles.title: Traders hold pig holiday to protest imports
articles.summary: Hog traders are implementing a three-day “pig holiday,” or a temporary suspension of the sale of pork, to protest the imports affecting the industry.

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 9:58pm
Hog traders are implementing a three-day “pig holiday,” or a temporary suspension of the sale of pork, to protest the imports affecting the industry.
In a 24 Oras report from Bernadette Reyes, the traders had already implemented the first day on Thursday.

“Gusto nating ipakita 'yung sitwasyon na wala ng karneng sariwang baboy sa palengke. 'Pag nakita nila 'yan, ‘ah, ito pala ang mangyayari kapag naubos ang mag-aalaga ng baboy,’ said Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines chairperson and AGAP Party-list Representative Nicanor Briones.
(We want to show our situation that there is no fresh pork in the wet market anymore. If they see that, ‘ah this is what will happen if the pig livestock runs out.)
According to the Pork Producers Federation of the Philippines, the industry is losing P350 million a day or P7,000 per pig head because of frozen pork coming from abroad.
However, several wet markets are not feeling the effects of the pig holiday.

“Nakikipag-coordinate naman yung boss ko sa DA (Department of Agriculture)... priority na we see to it na may supply araw-araw,” Poblacion Public Market Master Eva Araullo said. (We are coordinating with my boss at the DA… it is our priority that we see to it that there is a supply every day.)
It was also business as usual for Balintawak Market and the Marikina Public Market.
Sellers at a wet market in Mangaldan, Pangasinan also did not participate.
“Yung mga suki namin, ayaw lumayo. Tatlong araw 'yon, 'di kaya,” trader Marilou Velasquez said. (Our customers do not want to go far. That would be three days, we cannot.)
This was just the first day of the pig holiday. On the second holiday, traders will hold a protest in front of the DA.
However, the group Samahang Industriya ng Agrikultura (SINAG) will not partake in the protest. Instead, they will appeal to President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. directly.
“Lagpas na ito sa kamay ng DA, ang laban na ito nasa kamay na at nasa antas na ng Pangulo natin at ng kanyang mga economic managers,” SINAG Executive Director Jay Cainglet said.
(This is beyond the DA, this fight is in the hands of the President and his economic managers.)
The DA said that it understood the sentiments of the hog traders, but its hands were tied.

“Hindi namin basta-basta ma-control yan sa DA dahil those are under World Trade Organization agreements and bilateral agreements that were made before my time,” DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said.
(The DA could not just control that because those are under World Trade Organization agreements and bilateral agreements that were made before my time.)

The DA has already spoken with the Tariff Commission to return the tariffs on hogs. The agency is also studying the temporary suspension of hog imports for two months starting in November 2026. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

Government expects billions in extra tax revenue, but budget will remain tight
The German government expects to collect an extra €4.1 billion ($4.6 billion) in taxes next year, according to Finance Ministry calculations released Thursday.
When looking at the federal, state and communal levels, the increase is estimated to be over €10 billion, adding up to a total of €1 trillion paid in taxes in 2027.
However, Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the increased tax revenue would not bring relief to the budget.
Klingbeil said that despite "international crises and uncertainties," the German government was expecting a "stable trend" in tax revenue for 2026.

"We have responded to these crises. And we are in a robust position," Klingbeil said. For 2027, the government "will not gain any new fiscal leeway overall, but we also won’t have to close any new gaps."
He called for continued consolidation to protect future budgets.

articles.title: Makabayan Bloc urges recall of 2027 appropriations bill
articles.summary: The Makabayan Bloc in the House of Representatives on Thursday called on the House of Representatives to recall the 2027 House General Appropriations Bill to correct what its members said were…

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 9:45pm

The Makabayan Bloc in the House of Representatives on Thursday called on the House of Representatives to recall the 2027 House General Appropriations Bill to correct what its members said were unconstitutional provisions in the proposed national budget measure.
The call came after the Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts, as well as provisions on unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 GAA.

"Maaaring maging unconstitutional din ang 2027 GAA kung hindi po baguhin yung special provisions na ito. Kung hindi rin po makita na yung mga iskema na nabuyangyang na sa Korte Suprema ay uulitin lang dito sa 2027 GAA, baka ma-delay at hindi mapasa yung budget natin naayon sa batas," Kabataan Party-list Rep Renee Co said in an online press conference today.

"Kaya po ang panawagan ng Kabataan Party-list din, kasama ng Makabayan bloc, recall House Bill 10858 ng HoKabataan Party-list Rep Renee Co said in an online press conference today.use of Representatives," said Co, a lawyer.

(The 2027 General Appropriations Act could also be deemed unconstitutional if these special provisions are not amended. Furthermore, if it becomes apparent that the very schemes already struck down by the Supreme Court are simply being replicated in the 2027 GAA, the passage of our budget—in accordance with the law—could be delayed. For this reason, the Kabataan Party-list, together with the Makabayan bloc, calls for the recall of House Bill 10858.)

The House assistant minority leader said that if the House does not recall its version of the proposed 2027 national budget, the last opportunity to remove what she called illegal provisions in the 2027 GAB would be in the Senate or in the Bicameral Conference Committee.
GMA News has reached out to the House leadership and to House Committee on Appropriations Chair Rep Mikaela Suansing but has yet to receive a reply.
Gabriela Women's Party Rep Sarah Elago supported the Makabayan bloc's call.
"If the provisions and mechanisms that are already condemned or prohibited by the court remain in the 2027 Budget, they must be corrected before it is finally passed," Elago said.
"The Senate and the Bicameral Conference Committee must also ensure that no insertions are again hidden behind unclear allocations," Elago said during the online press conference," she added.
Co also called on the Ombudsman and the Commission on Audit to conduct investigations on the issue.

"Hinihimok din po namin ang ombudsman at COA to immediately pursue the authors, proponents, and implementers. Kasama rin po dito si Pangulong Marcos Jr. para sa mga liabilities under the operative fact doctrine's exclusion of bad faith officials," Co said.

"If the parties observed the law or implemented the law in bad faith or may attendance of bad faith sa execution of the law and its implementation, hindi po mapoprotektahan ng doctrine of operative fact yung mga implementers o yung mga partido," she added.

"So, ngayon, ano bang maaaring badges of bad faith? So preliminarily, and ito mas academic discussion na lang din, kasama po dyan yung BBM parametric formula. In clear text, sinasabi po ng essentially ng Malacanang through speaking through a department and in-observe in the budget na may priorities yung leadership," Co said.

(We also urge the ombudsman and COA to immediately pursue the authors, proponents, and implementers. This includes President Marcos Jr. for liabilities under the operative fact doctrine's exclusion of bad faith officials. If the parties observed the law or implemented the law in bad faith or had attendance of bad faith in the execution of the law and its implementation, the doctrine of operative fact cannot protect the implementers or the parties. So, what might constitute "badges of bad faith"? As a preliminary point—and this is more of an academic discussion—the "BBM parametric formula" could be considered one. In essence, Malacañang—speaking through a department and as reflected in the budget—is signaling that the current leadership has specific priorities.) —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Ilhan Omar says 'bizarre' pre-dawn raid on her home is forcing her to move out
articles.summary: The congresswoman said federal agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of a federal investigation.

blocks.text: Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar has said she can no longer live in her Washington DC home after it was searched by federal agents last week, fearing her address has been exposed after the raid.
"With the death threats that I deal with, it's not, it's no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids," she told MSN NOW, external.

In Omar's first public interview since the pre-dawn search of her home, she detailed how Homeland Security Investigations agents seized over a dozen items, including cell phones and notebooks, as part of an investigation.
The government has not said what crime Omar is accused of but that the raid was "part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation".
The search follows multiple comments from officials that cast doubt on Omar's US citizenship, which she received in 2000 after her arrival from Kenya.

More than a dozen subpoenas have also been issued to members of Omar's family, as part of the investigation, and it was reported that her personal computers and passport were among the items that were seized.
Recalling the hourslong raid of her home with MS NOW, Omar said: "It obviously did freak all of us out."
Omar said agents began "pounding on the doors" of her home at around 06:00 EDT (11:00 BST) on 12 October, startling her and her husband, who were both in bed.
"We were screaming," she said, as the couple ran downstairs to see what was happening, calling the incident "so bizarre".
The Minnesota Democrat estimated that between15 to 25 agents encircled her home, all of whom she said "conducted themselves in a decent way".
Agents presented Omar with a warrant at the door after she asked for one.

She then watched from the couch as agents spent roughly five hours going from room to room, Omar said, leaving with a total of 17 items, including multiple cellphones, notebooks, and her husband's camera from the 1960s.
The BBC contacted the Justice Department for comment after being referred by the DHS.
Omar again criticised the government's investigation, suggesting that it was meant to be intimidating.
Immediately following the raid last week, she posted a statement online where she called it "an outrageous abuse of power" and "weaponisation of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".
Former President Barack Obama has also blasted the federal probe, saying in a lengthy statement that it was "so appalling".
Omar, who has represented Minnesota since 2018, has long been a target of President Donald Trump's, who has repeatedly suggested she "go back" to Somalia.
He has denied any involvement in her investigation, saying it has "nothing to do with me".
At an Ohio rally in October, Trump referred to the search of her home, saying: "I don't know what they're doing with it, but I can tell you this: she's a disaster."
The congresswoman, however, rejected the president's response, arguing that "he's got everything to do with it".
"You know, this goes back to 2019 when he was screaming about the fact that, you know, I, I need to be sent back, I need to be deported."

articles.title: Caguioa vows to restore public trust in judiciary if named chief justice
articles.summary: Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa said Thursday that he wants to restore public trust in the judiciary if appointed chief justice of the Supreme Court.

blocks.text: Published October 22, 2026 9:30pm
Associate Justice Benjamin Caguioa said Thursday that he wants to restore public trust in the judiciary if appointed chief justice of the Supreme Court.

During his interview with the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC), Caguioa said the judiciary must redirect focus to the core value of the judiciary as an independent institution that should not be swayed by money or politics.
“My focus now really is the trial judges because they are the face of the judiciary. So I want the public to trust the judiciary. For me, there’s a lack of trust,” he said.
“Maybe that’s why they go to radio stations to complain. That, for me, says a lack of trust in the system,” he added.
Caguioa was part of the first batch of candidates interviewed for the position that will be vacated by Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo in November.
He said that if he is appointed, his colleagues can expect him to act the same.
“They know me… they know I’m straight… I simply follow the law. I don’t deviate. I respect the separation of powers. They can expect me to be the same,” he said.
When asked how he wanted to be remembered as a chief justice, if appointed, Caguioa said he wanted to be known as “just a decent guy.”

The JBC members present were Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, Senator Kiko Pangilinan, Batangas Representative Gerville Luistro, retired SC Associate Justice Jose Catral Mendoza, lawyer Nesauro Firme, retired Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Erlinda Piñera, and lawyer Jose Meija.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: France confirms first Shamonda virus infection in a human death of 'severely immunocompromised' individual
articles.summary: The Shomonda virus has been detected in a human for the first time, French health officials said. Authorities see no risk to the public, adding that the victim, who died in early October, was…

image.caption: French health officials say the livestock virus poses no theat to the public, pointing out that the first detected human infection was an exceedingly rare caseImage: Alexis Jumeau/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: French health officials on Thursday confirmed that they had detected the Shamonda virus in a human — who died early this month — in what they say was the first-ever case of a human contracting the livestock disease.

"Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," said France's Ministries of Health and of Agriculture in a joint statement.
"No health risk to the general public identified at this time," they said, adding that the human infection appeared to be, "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient."
How is Shamonda virus transmitted?

First ​identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the insect-borne Shamonda virus is a variant of the Orthobunyavirus, a genus that contains 138 species, and primarily affects livestock, ‌particularly cattle.
It is transmitted by culicoides, or biting midges.
The virus has been detected in ​animals in Africa and Japan for years and has been spreading across Europe this year.
Until now, it was not thought to be transmissible to humans.

According to a press statement on the Ministry of Agriculture's webpage, "At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the case resulted from vector-borne transmission via the bite of a culicoid midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was reported to be circulating among animals in the spring and summer of 2026."

The ministry said biological, clinical and epidemiological investigations are being carried out by experts in human, animal and environmental health, adding that authorities at the World Health Organization and European Center for Disease Control had been notified of the incident.

articles.title: ‘Justice is hope’: Here are Leonen’s 9 promises as aspiring chief justice
articles.summary: 'Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer.... On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,' says Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

blocks.text: LEONEN. Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen during the Judicial and Bar Council's public interviews for chief justice candidates on October 22, 2026.
Supreme Court of the Philippines
'Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer.... On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,' says Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen

items: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen presented nine promises aimed at enhancing the Philippine judiciary as he seeks to become the 28th chief justice.
Leonen emphasized the importance of an independent judiciary and the need for the court to serve the marginalized, promising to uphold accountability and accessibility in the justice system.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen gave not one, not two, but nine promises on Thursday, October 22, as he vies to become the country’s 28th Supreme Court (SC) chief justice.

Leonen was the first of five candidates to face the Judicial and Bar Council for its public interviews. Leonen said his plan includes a promise to enhance the expertise of judges and ensure that justice is accessible to everyone — especially the marginalized.

items: Improvement of judges Continuation of Unified Legal Aid Service (mandatory free legal service of lawyers), developmental and social change lawyering, program of remote hearings and translation. More exposure for judges to jails and communities “Judges at every level must remain open to the possibility that their premises are mistaken,” Leonen said.

Transparency in resolving cases When a case is submitted for decision, Leonen said the parties should be told the date by which the SC is expected to decide on it. If the date won’t be met, the parties should be told why.

Continued digitalization of courts Leonen said the entire justice system should be digitalized — from the Department of Justice’s prosecution, trials at regional trial courts, to the appellate courts and SC.

Accountability in public office Quicker resolution of corruption cases “Every case already filed by the Office of the Ombudsman arising from large-scale corruption decided at first instance before the end of 2027, the horizon of our Strategic Plan,” Leonen said.
Consultation with business sector Review of regulatory actions and reporting of alleged exactions or extortions by any court official or employee

Creation of more courts Leonen said at least 10 halls of justice should be built in the country’s poorest provinces. “Where no building will ever be close enough, our court will travel, as it did from Bongao to Simunul, Tawi-Tawi,” he added.
Court’s independence If he becomes chief justice, Leonen said the SC will publicize any attempts at interference, who the court officials and employees met, about what, and what was asked.

Creation of laws for those who need it Review Batas Pambansa Bilang 129 and consolidate the Rules of Court and the special rules into a Philippine Code of Pleading and Practice. Rules on the customary law of the indigenous peoples Writ of Kalayaan, which will compel “agencies responsible for a detention facility to act on its conditions, together and in the open”
A review of the legal profession Review on the admission to the Bar Improvements for Shari’ah (Islamic law) counselors and lawyers

blocks.text: Leonen said he will continue Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo’s plan to innovate the judiciary.

“I offer all these, with my faults and weaknesses, which I constantly try to overcome. The ideas we debate today and the personalities who will appear before you pale in comparison to this: our people still suffer,” the aspiring chief justice said.

“Whoever is appointed, this reality remains: our people still suffer. Yet they still come to our courts, holding their folders and their receipts, because they have decided that this is where their grievance belongs. On our watch, we cannot fail them. I will not fail them,” he added.

blocks.caption: ‘Justice is hope’: Here are Leonen’s 9 promises as aspiring chief justice

blocks.text: Leonen said that in these times of political and economic challenges, the Philippines needs a chief magistrate who is independent and ready to make hard decisions for the people.

He believes a chief justice should protect the confidentiality of SC deliberations, encourage other justices to speak up about their opinions, explain the Court’s decisions fully, and protect dissent.

“All this because the judiciary should be where government is held to its conscience, the Constitution. A judiciary beholden to powerful interests — past, present, or future — does not deserve its name,” the senior magistrate said.

Leonen said he will be, if ever, an independent chief justice, as proven by his track record. He said he has been senior associate justice for nearly 14 years and has worked with 5 chief justices and 37 associate justices.
According to him, he has been an acting chief justice on many occasions and has chaired the SC’s 2nd and 3rd Divisions, among others.

“I have voted, on principle, against the legal positions of the President who appointed me, and of every President who has sat since. I have also written unanimous decisions that clarified the framework and limits of the discretion of powerful departments and officials in government,” Leonen said.
“I do not say this to my credit. It is the only assurance worth anything to the public,” he added

Leonen said the court’s success will be measured by whether the poorest litigants can rely on it, if they can tell their families the justice system gave them a fighting chance in a case. He also believes that court decisions should reach and be understood by everyone.

The chief magistrate added that lawyers should think of empowering people. As officers of the court, Leonen said they should explain what the law is, why the law is the way it is, and what could be done about it.

“Justice is hope. Hope is honored when a remedy is owed to a named person, by a date, and then delivered. Anything short of that reduces hope to a mere sentiment. Our people have been offered sentiments for a very long time,” Leonen said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Nunchucks’ wielded by agitated man in Hannah Beazley’s office may have been drumsticks, court told
articles.summary:
John Lawrence Smart charged with being armed in a way that may cause fear but Perth lawyer expresses concern for mental health

  • Get our

blocks.text: A man accused of making threats while armed with “improvised nunchucks” at a Western Australian MP’s electorate office could have been holding a musical instrument, not a weapon, a court has been told.
John Lawrence Smart appeared on Thursday in the WA magistrates court where his lawyer expressed concern for his mental health. He was not required to enter a plea.
Smart was accused of making verbal threats at the office of state Labor MP Hannah Beazley in the inner-Perth suburb of Victoria Park on Wednesday afternoon.

He was charged on Thursday with being armed in a way that may cause fear, making an unlawful threat and possessing cannabis. Police alleged Smart “made verbal threats while in possession of an improvised martial arts weapon (nunchucks)”.
During the court hearing, the highly agitated 56-year-old held his head in his hands and said he had been a musician for 20 years and he was holding claves.

blocks.caption: Police allege John Lawrence Smart was armed with improvised nunchucks but a Perth magistrate asked if they could have been drumsticks. Photograph: WA police

blocks.text: “People, they don’t understand what I’m going through,” he said from the dock. Smart claimed people had “destroyed” his head.
Prosecutors said Smart entered Beazley’s office physically agitated and screaming, and holding two pieces of wood tied together.
He had a second similar implement attached to his belt, the police prosecutor said.
Smart allegedly demanded to see the politician while raising one of the implements above his head in a threatening manner before leaving the premises.
Smart’s lawyer said he was known to carry percussion sticks in the community and play drums.
The magistrate Heidi Watson suggested to the prosecutor that Smart might have been holding “drumsticks”.
The court heard Smart had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia and displayed delusional persecutory beliefs. He believed he had the “devil inside him”.
Watson ordered that Smart remained in custody for further medical assessment.
Beazley earlier said two of her staff were present in the electorate office when Smart allegedly entered.
“It was confronting,” she said in a social media post. “My staff did an amazing job and did everything right.”
No one was injured in the alleged incident, which comes after federal member for Indi Helen Haines was struck by a 4WD vehicle outside her electorate office in northern Victoria on Monday.
after newsletter promotion
That incident sparked a nationwide debate about whether public officials were sufficiently protected from threats against their safety.
The WA premier, Roger Cook, said state parliament had been shocked by both incidents.
“We have got to start to turn the temperature down,” he said.
Cook said discussions were under way about potential upgrades to security measures to protect parliamentarians and their staff.
“Everyone deserves to feel safe at work, at home and in their communities,” he said.
“It’s not OK for people to take out their aggressions, their disagreements on staff in a politician’s office.”
Cook said security measures could be improved at state parliament, but they must be balanced with the need to maintain public access.
The Labor leader said he would support making an allowance available to MPs for security upgrades at their homes.
Beazley is the Labor state minister for local government and the daughter of former federal Labor leader Kim Beazley.
Smart was scheduled to return to the same court next Thursday.

articles.title: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors say
articles.summary: Assessment finds global heating is endangering 96% of coral reefs across 80 countries – a figure scientists say should serve as a ‘wake-up call’
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet, including Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, faces a high risk of ecosystem collapse before 2075 because of global heating, according to an assessment by United Nations nature advisers.
About 24% of the planet’s reefs across more than 80 countries are already critically endangered, the assessment said, but when the expected impacts of global heating were added this rose to 96%.

Coral reefs are known as the rainforests of the sea. A quarter of all known marine species are found in and around them and they support hundreds of millions of people with food, as well as protecting shorelines and supporting tourism.

Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and global heating have already caused declines in the ecosystems over the past 50 years, measured by the loss of live coral as well as changes in fish populations, the assessment said.

But the scientists said while the prognosis was dire, the findings should serve as a “wake-up call” because reefs could survive with rapid cuts to fossil fuel use and strong conservation action at local levels.
“The risk is real and very concerning,” said Dr Mishal Gudka, research director at CORDIO (Coral Reef Degradation in the Indian Ocean) East Africa and the scientific lead for the assessment.
“We stand to lose one of the most valuable ecosystems we have – the impacts of which will affect millions of people around the world.”

The assessment analysed the current status and future threat levels of 127 coral reef regions and was coordinated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), an international group that advises the United Nations.

The assessment assumed greenhouse gas emissions – mainly from burning fossil fuels – would follow a “middle-of-the-road” pathway, causing about 2.7C of global heating by the end of the century when compared with temperatures before the Industrial Revolution.
Current climate policies and targets adopted by countries around the world are likely to cause about 2.6C of global heating, one assessment finds.

The share of coral eco-regions considered critically endangered would likely be even higher, the IUCN said, but four regions did not have enough data to assess them and the coral reefs of the western Galápagos had already collapsed.

blocks.caption: Extensive coral bleaching occurred at the Ningaloo Reef, WA, in February 2025. Photograph: Brooke Pyke

blocks.text: The critically endangered classification meant an “extremely high risk” of ecosystem collapse before 2075.
The group considers a coral reef ecosystem to have collapsed if the reef could not maintain itself because of a near or complete loss of living reef-building corals.

The assessment did not fully account for the impacts of the fourth global mass bleaching event from early 2023 to mid-2025 – the most widespread global mass bleaching event on record, the US government’s Coral Reef Watch has confirmed.
That global event was bookended by the worst mass bleaching event on record for reefs in Western Australia where a heatwave killed corals across 1,500 kilometres (930 miles).
after newsletter promotion

Marine heatwaves can cause corals to separate from the symbiotic algae that provides them with colour and nutrient. While not always deadly, bleaching can weaken corals and make them more susceptible to disease.
Gudka said the results were a “wake-up call” and were “alarming, but certainly not hopeless”.
He said: “They should be seen as a call to action – an early warning sign before the worst outcomes eventuate.”

Dr Grethel Aguilar, the director general of the IUCN, said: “It is not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover, but it requires decisive action to tackle climate change and halt further ocean warming.

“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them.”
Four of Australia’s 17 reef regions were considered critically endangered. Five were endangered and five more were classed as vulnerable.
But all 17 regions, including the Great Barrier Reef, were critically endangered once the expected impacts of climate change were accounted for.

Dr Ben Fitzpatrick of the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute led the Australian assessment. He said even after accounting for the ability of some corals to adapt to warmer water, the rising heat “overwhelmed everything”.

“Reefs are like Picasso paintings underwater,” he said. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives.
“To think we might lose that is devastating. There’s one message. We have to stop burning fossil fuels.”

MANILA, Philippines – P-pop meets history at Rappler Live Jam on Thursday, October 22, with the cast of Gregoria Lakambini: A Pinay Pop Musical!
Gregoria Lakambini tells the story of Gregoria de Jesus — who is known as Ka Oryang or the Mother of the Philippine Revolution — and her eventual growth as the Lakambini of the Katipunan.

In the musical, Marynor Madamesila takes on the titular role of Gregoria de Jesus. It also stars Anya Evangelista (ensemble and Andres Bonifacio), Heart Puyong (ensemble and Emilio Aguinaldo), Sofia Sacaguing (ensemble and Julio Nakpil), Sarah Monay (ensemble and Gregoria de Jesus understudy), Ynna Rafa (ensemble), Murline Uddin (ensemble), and Frances Marie (swing).
The show was first staged by Tanghalang Pilipino in 2025. This year, it is returning from November 13 to 29 at the Proscenium Theater in Makati City.

articles.title: Grandparent hugging consent ad pulled after criticism
articles.summary: Jim O'Callaghan described the video as "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".

blocks.text: The Irish minister for justice has criticised an advertisement produced by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) promoting consent, calling it "inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents".
The ad depicts two grandparents enthusiastically hugging a young boy, but when they approach their granddaughter she appears unhappy about the exchange.
It includes the message "not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them".
The ad, which has since been removed, has attracted criticism and and also received international coverage in publications such as the New York Post.
Fianna Fáil politician Jim O'Callaghan, whose department funds the campaign, said the the video has since been removed following engagement with the DRCC.
He said the video "does not represent the views of the Government".
"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them.
"While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."
The video was part of a campaign titled 'We-Consent', which is led by the DRCC.

In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said: "We-Consent is a long-term campaign as part of Dublin Rape Crisis Centre's prevention work to increase the awareness and practice of consent in Ireland.
"We created three videos premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too.
"We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have."

As well as the Department of Justice, the 'We-Consent' campaign is also supported by the Department of Children, Equality, Disability, Integration and Youth, and CUAN (the Domestic, Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Agency).
All three have been approached for comment.
Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill said the video was a waste of resources.
"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said.

"The issue of consent is a very serious one and I acknowledge the important work the Rape Crisis Centre and other agencies do every day to advocate for all victims of rape and sexual violence, including children.
"But this publicly funded social media video is a million miles off the mark."
He added: "What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"

A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said: "'We-Consent' is a programme created and developed by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre, aimed at informing, educating, and engaging the public about all forms of consent.
"Social media videos shared recently as part of this programme were produced by DRCC at a low-cost using volunteers and are not part of a Government advertising campaign.
"The Department understands that DRCC intends to review these videos. They are being removed from their social media channels to enable this review."

articles.title: Iran's Balochistan border region sees growing unrest
articles.summary: Violence is on the rise in Iran's border region with Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Iran war could shift the strategic balance for militant groups operating in the area.

image.caption: Iranian military forces are present in the southeastern border region Image: Farhikhtegan

blocks.text: Recent weeks have seen renewed attacks, assassinations and armed clashes in the southeastern province bordering Pakistan and Afghanistan. The incidents occurred in the provincial capital of Zahedan, as well as smaller border towns.

The border region of Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan is home to the Baloch ethnic minority. The region on either side of the Iran-Pakistan border is among the most economically disadvantaged of the wider area.
The Pakistani province of Balochistan is economically underdeveloped, despite having large reserves of natural gas, gold and copper.

The situation is similarly dire in the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchistan, which is predominantly inhabited by Sunni Baluchis. It is one of the poorest regions in the country and marked by underdeveloped infrastructure, limited educational opportunities and water supply shortages.
Significantly less information is available about the situation of the Baloch in Afghanistan.
Armed groups sense security gaps
Various Baloch groups are active in Iran and Pakistan, some of whom seek Balochistan independence. Yet to date, there is no evidence of coordinated cross-border cooperation among these organizations.

In December 2025, several Baloch opposition groups in Iran united under the umbrella of the Popular Fighters Front. Observers see this as an attempt to more closely integrate their political and military activities.
This coalition, which formed before the outbreak of the Iran war, could try to exploit security gaps created by the current situation, Iranian journalist Mehdi Nakhl Ahmadi told DW.
Ahmadi, who lives in Italy, has been covering the situation of the Baloch people for years. He said the new security situation could allow armed groups to expand their operations.
Struggling with poverty, suffering marginalization

Ahmadi said there are structural reasons for Baloch dissatisfaction. "The Islamic Republic's security policy toward ethnic and religious regions has widened the gap in economic development between these regions and other parts of the country in recent decades," he said.
He added that the rising number of attacks points to a shift in dynamics, as do increased coordination and changes in the way recent operations have been carried out.
Among the victims of recent clashes were members of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, the Basij militia, armed individuals, and a Sunni cleric.

A source within Iran, who is familiar with the situation of the Baloch people, yet whose identity we cannot disclose security for reasons, attributed some of the armed violence to political, economic and religious discontent.
Discrimination in employment, education, regional development and religious matters contribute to the tension, the source said.
Hidden executions surge in Iran during US-Israeli war

That's why the armed conflict should not be viewed in isolation, the Iranian source explained. Clergy, academics and other social leaders had been trying for years to peacefully voice their demands for better social policies and greater investment in the region, the source said.
The fact that these efforts were largely unsuccessful had led to a growing willingness among some to resort to more radical measures.
"The high number of executions in recent decades is another factor that fuels discontent," said the source. Most documented executions in the province, meanwhile, are related to drug offenses.

Although Baluchis make only up an estimated 2–6% of the Iranian population, they are significantly overrepresented among those put to death. Iran Human Rights reports that Baluchis accounted for 9% of all recorded executions in 2025. In previous years, that figure was 11% (2024) and 20% (2023), respectively.

For many people who live in this economically disadvantaged region, smuggling opium into Iran, and fuel out of the country, are one of the few ways to earn a living. This, in turn, has contributed to a continued military and security presence at the border.
It is not, meanwhile, known whether armed groups in southeastern Iran are being supported from abroad.

blocks.caption: For many people in the region, fuel smuggling across the Iran-Pakistan border is one of the few ways to make a livingImage: Abdula Ghani Kakar/DW

blocks.text: Violence has also escalated in the Pakistani province of Balochistan. According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, 131 armed attacks were recorded there in September, up from 89 in August.

In addition to the separatist movement, which has been active for years, the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) are also expanding their operations. This had led to strategically important transportation links between Iran and Pakistan coming under growing pressure.
Still, it cannot be said with certainty whether the recent uptick in violence in Iran's Sistan and Baluchistan province stems from security gaps resulting from the Iran war.
The growing number of attacks does, however, suggests that the security situation in the already fragile border region continues to deteriorate.
Additional reporting by Morad Rahmati.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Carney announces trade and defence partnership with Turkey
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, right, walks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as he arrives at the Bestepe Presidential complex in Ankara, Turkey, on Thursday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking

Prime Minister Mark Carney's political and economic tightrope act began Thursday as he and Turkish President Recep Erdogan announced a strategic partnership aimed at expanding trade and defence co-operation.
PM visits Ankara seeking stronger ties with key NATO ally
It is the latest step in the warming of relations between the two nations and an important moment in the prime minister's plan to co-operate more closely with other middle-power countries.
Carey praised Turkey as an "exceptional" partner.
"No country builds strength alone," he said in a joint statement at the sprawling presidential palace compound.

"The most resilient countries bring together complementary strengths with trusted partners. Our goal isn’t self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience. That’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for Canadians."
There are four pillars to the new partnership — trade and investment, defence and security, energy, and people-to-people ties.

Next month, negotiators will sit down in Ankara for the first round of free trade talks. Also, the partnership includes a new agreement on defence industry co-operation that will better connect Canadian and Turkish companies.
Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson, seen here in Ottawa on July 16, will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

The partnership will also pave the way for investments in the energy and critical minerals sectors. The two countries will also finalize an air transport agreement, increasing passenger flights between the two countries.

The bilateral visit, a first for Canadian prime minister, comes as human rights groups raise the alarm over Turkey's sweeping crackdown last month on dissent and civil society groups, including the dismantling of 2SLGBTQ+ and HIV-advocacy organizations.

"The prime minister has been very clear. We need to engage with the world as it is, not the way we wish it to be," Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said ahead of the trip. He will be joining Carney for talks with Turkish officials.
People run from the police during a march in support of transgender people and their rights during the 2SLGBTQ+ Pride week, in Istanbul, Turkey, on June 21. (Dilara Acikgoz/The Associated Press)
"Where we have differences of opinion, we discuss those in private."

Carney is looking to diversify Canada's trade to make the country less dependent on the United States. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific.

Turkey, a member of NATO with a growing defence industrial sector, is seen as a key ally on the trade and military production fronts, says Thomas Juneau of the University of Ottawa, an expert in the Middle East.
"What the Carney government appears to be making as a choice is not to restrict diversification efforts only to democracies, only to countries that have positive human rights records," said Juneau.
Turkey has become increasingly authoritarian under Erdogan, who has been president since 2014.

"This is morally a difficult dilemma on the Canadian side, but the calculus appears on the part of the government that if Canada were to choose to diversify only with democracies the ceiling for success would be low."
Immediately after landing in Ankara on Thursday, visited Anitkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, who was the founder and first president of the Republic of Turkey.

The structure and its 750,000 square-metre grounds are beautifully maintained, divided into the Peace Park with tens of thousands of plants and trees including Canadian maples, and the Monument Block. Carney laid a wreath at the monument.
Carney pays his respects after laying a wreath during a ceremony at the Anıtkabir, the Mausoleum of Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, in Ankara. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
Turkey aims to expand its energy capacity significantly in the coming decades, planning to add roughly 20 gigawatts of nuclear power by 2050.

To that end, Ottawa and Ankara are reportedly planning to set up a working group to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's Candu nuclear team in order to build Turkey's planned second or third nuclear power plant.
Hodgeson declined comment on the possibility.

items: Carney's Turkish balancing act must include business, defence and human rights
Turkey's president gifted Carney a revolver at NATO summit. Carney gave him maple syrup

blocks.text: Sevag Belian, the executive director of the Armenian National Committee of Canada, says any nuclear deal with Turkey deserves close scrutiny.

He pointed to the previous falling out between the two countries which resulted in Canada imposing a de facto arms embargo, which was mostly lifted in 2024. The lifting of those measures was the price Erdogen demanded of the Trudeau government for getting behind Sweden's membership in NATO.
The fallout started in 2020 when Turkish authorities applied for an exemption related to importation of Wescam target acquisition gear used in Turkey's Bayraktar drones.

"We know from the disclosed documents that they had said that they will be using the few cameras that they got through the exemption for reconnaissance activities related to NATO operations in the north of Syria," said Belian.
"But then we know that those cameras were actually diverted illegally to Azerbaijan and used during the war in Nagorno.
"We have established through parliamentary investigation that the Turkish side clearly lied."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.
